blocks.text: LESSON 1
AN INTRODUCTION
Scripture Text: Romans 12:3-8
DAILY READINGS
☐ Monday: 2 Kings 2:9-15 ☐ Tuesday: 1 Corinthians 12:28-31 ☐ Wednesday: Ephesians 4:7-12 ☐ Thursday: Romans 12:3-8 ☐ Friday: 1 Corinthians 12:1, 7-11 ☐ Saturday: Proverbs 25:14; Proverbs 18:16
MEMORY VERSE: But covet earnestly the best gifts. —1 Corinthians 12:31

I have a dual burden behind this study: (1) to instruct (as "all scripture is given ... for instruction"; 2 Timothy 3:16), and (2) that through exposure to these truths, desire might be created within you to "covet earnestly the best gifts" (1 Corinthians 12:31) so that "a man [might] desire the office" (1 Tim-othy 3:1). For the truth to be perpetuated until our Lord returns requires the continual operation of spiritual gifts in the filling of ecclesiastical offices. The Apostle Paul said in Romans 11:29, "For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance." The Expanded Greek Translation of the New Testa-ment renders it, "For the gifts in grace at the calling of God are with respect to a change of mind irrevocable."

The gifts and offices that led to the successful operation of the primitive church are just as vitally needed for the church's successful operation today. As revered leaders step off the stage of action, gifts do not die with them. Just as Elijah's mantle fell upon Elisha (2 Kings 2:13-15), so God's plan to-day is to call and prepare successive leadership. However, it is important to note that Elisha coveted the gift Elijah had (2 Kings 2:9) and desired to fill his office. God is looking for just such ones today.

Ezekiel 22:30 reads, "And I sought for a man among them." It is our bur-den, as you study these lessons, that not only will "the eyes of your under-standing ... [be] enlightened" (Ephesians 1:18) but also that a desire will be created to "covet earnestly the best gifts" (1 Corinthians 12:31), that we may see no office deficient or lacking.
Gifts and Offices

Romans 12:6 Having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us. There are different gifts. First Corinthians 12:8-9 says, "To one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowl-edge ... To another faith ... to another the gifts of healing" and so forth. Not all receive the same gifts, and there is a valid reason it is ordained that way. The gift is the talent or ability that equips one to fill a particular office. It would be difficult to be called as one of the "teachers" (1 Corinthians 12:28; Ephesians 4:11) and not have "the word of knowledge" (1 Corinthians 12:8), or to be "called to be an apostle" (Romans 1:1) without the gift of "faith" (1 Corinthians 12:9). The gifts equip the persons for the offices the Lord de-sires they fill.

The Apostle Paul said in Romans 11:13, "I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I magnify mine office." First Timothy 3:1 declares, "If a man desire the of-fice of a bishop, he desireth a good work." Ephesians 4:11 gives a listing of the ministerial offices in the church: "some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers." Five offices are listed. (Some scholars question whether "teachers" is a separate category, but 1 Corinthians 12:28 explains it is a separate office.) Each office is essential. Without the operation of each of these offices, the church will be deficient and handicapped, as a body with a missing member.

Romans 12:4 All members have not the same office. The different gifts are placed in different offices. The church is operated through these offices. In sectarianism, men who do not have the gifts fill offices, and the results are tragic. The wise man said, "Whoso boasteth himself of a false gift is like clouds and wind without rain" (Proverbs 25:14). This is why Babylon is so dry and parched. Conversely, the Lord does not want a man on whom He be-stows gifts and talents to hide his "talent in the earth" (Matthew 25:25), but to be willing so that his "gift maketh room for him" (Proverbs 18:16). This requires making the personal sacrifice required to step up and fill the office, or offices, the Lord may be calling him to fill.
Many Members—One Body

Romans 12:4 We have many members in one body. One of the most famous and frequent analogies the Apostle Paul used regarding the church is that of a body. The church is one body, but as with the natural body, for it to function properly requires the operation of many members. There must ever be a spirit of cooperation among the many members. Each member
must recognize the importance of the role of the others and "should have the same care one for another" (1 Corinthians 12:25).

We also must recognize that because there are different gifts, the grace that is given to us (Romans 12:6) is in relation to our gift. We should fill the office that coincides with our gifts. For example, one may have the gift to fill the office of an evangelist and have a tremendous ability in that area, yet lack "the word of wisdom" (1 Corinthians 12:8) necessary to be a suc-cessful pastor. Much havoc has been brought about over the years by people not abiding in their calling. Grace is only given for the particular gift that we possess.

Romans 12:3 Think soberly, according as God hath dealt to every man the measure of faith. Ephesians 4:7 reads, "But unto every one of us is given grace according to the measure of the gift of Christ." There is grace only in proportion to the gift given. When one steps outside the bounds of that gift, the grace is not operational. Therefore, while it behooves us to "covet earnestly the best gifts" (1 Corinthians 12:31), we must also have an understanding of the gifts we possess and abide within their bounds. Those gifts will prepare us for service in particular offices, but we must be cautious that neither our zeal causes us to overstep our gifts, nor our hesitance causes us to fail to step up when the Spirit of God directs.

In this quarterly, we will study what a gift actually is, what it is used for, and how we are to use it. Also, we will study the various offices that must be filled for the successful operation of the church. It is my desire that we study these truths so that each of us will have the keen sense that we truly need to have "an ear [to] ... hear what the Spirit saith" (Revelation 2:7).
JUST A THOUGHT
He who steps out of the boundary of his gift leaves himself open for the enemy to sift!

blocks.text: LESSON 2
GIFTS
Scripture Texts: 1 Corinthians 12:1; Ephesians 4:7-8
DAILY READINGS

☐ Monday: 1 Corinthians 1:4-8 ☐ Tuesday: Matthew 25:15; 1 Corinthians 12:11 ☐ Wednesday: 1 Corinthians 7:7; 1 Peter 4:10-11 ☐ Thursday: Ephesians 4:16; 1 Corinthians 7:20 ☐ Friday: 1 Corinthians 14:12 ☐ Saturday: Matthew 5:6
MEMORY VERSE: Now concerning spiritual gifts, brethren, I would not have you ignorant. —1 Corinthians 12:1

In this lesson, we will examine the gifts. In 1 Corinthians 12:1, the Apos-tle Paul penned, "Now concerning spiritual gifts, brethren, I would not have you ignorant." Though the congregation in Corinth came "behind in no gift" (or as one rendering says, "There is no gift in which you are deficient"; 1 Co-rinthians 1:7), they were lacking understanding concerning these "gifts" and their proper operation. Certainly, if this congregation in the first century (where all these gifts were operating) needed teaching, it is even more crucial for the church in the twenty-first century (that is shedding the effects of the sectarian taint of the cloudy day, Protestantism) to receive clear instruction concerning these gifts.
What Is a Spiritual Gift?

1 Corinthians 12:1 Now concerning spiritual gifts ... I would not have you ignorant. One rendering says, "Not right for you to be without teach-ing." Notice the Apostle denoted these as spiritual gifts. One translation of-fers this passage as, "I do not want you to be ignorant about manifestations of the Spirit." The Greek word for "spiritual" in our text is pneumatikos. It literally means "non-carnal, supernatural." This word does not appear in the Greek Septuagint or the Gospels. It is a post-Pentecost word, indicating those things that have their origin with God and therefore are in harmony with His character. It describes the qualities that proceed from God's nature and are produced in the saint's life through the Spirit of God.

Therefore, gifts that are truly spiritual gifts have a spiritual nature. The Scripture here is not speaking of masons, carpenters, or other physical incli-nations or talents. Certainly, children of God will sanctify these abilities to the work of God, serving as great blessings; but these types of abilities are not what is being dealt with in this text.

The word gifts is charisma in the original Greek. Outside of the New Testament, this word was not in common usage. In classical Greek, it was rarely used. In the New Testament, it is characteristically Paul's word. This word charisma occurs seventeen times—fourteen in the Pauline letters, twice in the Pastoral Epistles (also written by Paul), and once in 1 Peter. The meaning of this word is that of a free and undeserved gift, something that comes from God's nature, conveyed by God's grace, and given to God's peo-ple. It could never have been achieved, attained, or possessed by any human effort.
Who Has Spiritual Gifts?

Are these spiritual gifts for a spiritually elite group of people? Who is able to have these spiritual gifts? Consider the word used by Jesus in Mat-thew 25:15 where He declared He gave "to every man according to his sever-al ability." Jesus indicated that "every man" receives a talent. In 1 Corinthi-ans 7:7, the Apostle Paul substantiated this, penning, "But every man hath his proper gift of God." In 1 Corinthians 12:11, the sacred writer revealed the encouraging truth that "the selfsame Spirit" divides to "every man sever-ally as he will." Not only does "every" saint receive a spiritual gift, but they are given "according to his several ability" (the word severally means "spe-cially assigned"; The New Analytical Greek Lexicon). What a beautiful, in-spiring truth! The Emphatic Greek Diaglott says "according to his RESPEC-TIVE capacity."

Ephesians 4:7 Unto every one of us is given grace according to the measure of the gift of Christ. As children of God, we are "all the members of that one body" (1 Corinthians 12:12), "the church" (Colossians 1:18). Since every member has a gift as part of the one body, "every joint supplieth" (Ephesians 4:16); every member ministers to a need or provides a function in the church by the operation of that particular gift. Keep in mind, although "every one of us" has a gift, not everyone fills the offices mentioned in Ephe-sians 4:11.

Though it requires "gifts" to be qualified to fill an office, many who have these spiritual gifts do not fill the particular offices mentioned there. For example, in Romans 12:8, the Apostle listed the gift of giving. Certainly, one

may have this gift and yet never receive a call to be "apostles ... prophets ... evangelists ... pastors and teachers" (Ephesians 4:11). This reveals that all the gifts supply a vital part to the body of Christ and that each member and the operation of his or her gift is vital. Although he or she may not hold an office that is particularly mentioned, the operation of his or her gift is vital to the successful operation of the body.
The Operation of the Gifts

It should always be remembered that any gift you may have is just that—a gift from God (James 1:17). It is nothing of which you should be proud or boastful. The Apostle Paul declared, "But by the grace of God I am what I am" (1 Corinthians 15:10). The gift should be operated humbly, "in honour preferring one another" (Romans 12:10), allowing the gift to make room for itself (Proverbs 18:16). Also, we should not allow jealousy or envy to work, as the Lord apportions "according to his RESPECTIVE capacity" (Matthew 25:15; The Emphatic Greek Diaglott). In His wisdom, the Lord knows which gifts we are best matched to by our temperament, emotional composition, and physical abilities.

We should not be selfish with our gifts. First Corinthians 12:7 tells us, "But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal." One translation says "that he may use it for the common good." Another says "for the profit of all." The gift each saint possesses is not for his or her own selfish benefit. Rather, as Paul told the Corinthians, "Forasmuch as ye are zealous of spiritual gifts, seek that ye may excel to the edifying of the church" (1 Corinthians 14:12). The Amplified Bible Classic states, "Since you are so eager and ambitious to possess spiritual endowments and mani-festations of the [Holy] Spirit, [concentrate on] striving to excel and to abound [in them] in ways that will build up the church." Any time we seek to operate our gifts, it should be divinely prompted, in divine order, and for the benefit and edification of the body.
Dividing to Every Man

In 1 Corinthians 12:11, notice the particular wording that the Apostle em-ployed. He declared the Spirit is "dividing [a present tense verb] to every man." This is a continual and ongoing work of the Spirit in the church throughout every period of time. Not only is He giving gifts and abilities to the newly saved as they are added to the church, but in view of the Apostle's admonition to "covet earnestly the best gifts" (1 Corinthians 12:31), if we "hunger and thirst after righteousness" (Matthew 5:6), we "shall be filled."

If we "covet earnestly" what the Spirit is still "dividing," we can receive additional gifts. What an encouraging thought! We can desire more spiritual gifts. God is desirous to impart them for the betterment of His body. May we never be satisfied but ever strive for "the best gifts."
JUST A THOUGHT
If one does not use his gift to "profit withal," sadly, it will not profit at all!

blocks.text: LESSON 3
WISDOM AND KNOWLEDGE
Scripture Text: 1 Corinthians 12:1-8
DAILY READINGS

☐ Monday: Psalm 87:1-7 ☐ Tuesday: Acts 4:13-21 ☐ Wednesday: 2 Chronicles 1:10; Daniel 1:17; Proverbs 8:1; Proverbs 4:5 ☐ Thursday: Acts 6:1-10, 15 ☐ Friday: Acts 18:24-28 ☐ Saturday: 1 Corinthians 3:5-11
MEMORY VERSE: Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding. —Proverbs 4:7

Beginning with this lesson, we want to examine two particular gifts spe-cifically mentioned in the New Testament. In our text, as well as in Romans 12:6-8, the Apostle Paul enumerated specific spiritual gifts. In these listings, the divine penman was certainly not implying the list is exhaustive or entire. Certainly, these gifts are central and crucial to the successful operation of the New Testament church. However, it is also evident these passages are not all-inclusive of all gifts. The psalmist prophesied in Psalm 87:7, "The singers [and] ... the players on instruments shall be there." There are indeed those who are especially gifted to be one of "the singers" or "the players."

In the Parable of the Talents, we read the gifts are distributed "according to his several ability" (Matthew 25:15). This verse says, "And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one." Thus, the apportion-ment rests with the divine, and some may receive "several" gifts. These gifts possessed by various members of the body of Christ are for a twofold pur-pose: "mak[ing] increase of the body" and "the edifying of itself" (Ephesians 4:16).
As we view the specific gifts mentioned in the Pauline epistles, we also want to see how they were practically performed by the morning-time breth-ren who held various offices.
The Word of Wisdom
1 Corinthians 12:8 For to one is given by the Spirit the word of wis-dom. We must be reminded that these gifts are given. We are not talking

about natural abilities, inclinations, or propensities, but we are talking about "gifts." In the beginning of the Gospel Day, the ministry had a number of what was termed "unlearned and ignorant men" (Acts 4:13). The average high school graduate today is probably much better educated than many of the initial morning-time ministers. Yet, they "turned the world upside down" (Acts 17:6).

Verse 8 speaks of the word of wisdom. The Greek word for "wisdom" is sophia. It means "the insight into the true nature of things." The ancient church father, Clement of Alexandria, said it is "the knowledge of things both human and divine and of their cause." Sophia is the ultimate understanding and insight into matters both human and divine that can only come from a di-vine source. It enables us to understand beyond the realm of human compre-hension and to perceive realities as they are in the spiritual and eternal scheme. It enables the possessor of this ability or gift to act accordingly.

Solomon prayed for sophia: "Give me now wisdom [sophia]" (2 Chron-icles 1:10). Daniel and the three Hebrew children had this wisdom as well: "God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom" (Daniel 1:17). This particular attribute is crying for men to seek it: "Doth not wis-dom cry? and understanding put forth her voice?" (Proverbs 8:1). The wise man admonished us, "Get wisdom, get understanding" (Proverbs 4:5).

Let us view this gift in its New Testament setting. When the first deacons were selected in the New Testament, the qualifications were: "men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom" (Acts 6:3). Wisdom is a vital gift to the successful operation of the church. When Stephen, one of the seven deacons, disputed with the Jews, "they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake" (Acts 6:10).

The Apostle Paul said he was "a wise masterbuilder" (1 Corinthians 3:10). The wise man said, "Wisdom hath builded her house" (Proverbs 9:1). We know this "house" is the church (Hebrews 3:6; 1 Timothy 3:15). The Apostle Paul was successful because he had the gift of wisdom. This was ev-ident in how he turned the Pharisees and Sadducees against each other and diverted their attention away from him (Acts 23:6-10) and in how he admin-istered church discipline (1 Corinthians 5:13; 2 Corinthians 2:6-8).

Paul's wisdom and patient teaching of newly established congregations is seen in Colossians 1:3-9. Wisdom is an essential gift necessary to fill the office of an apostle or to sow new congregations. Certainly, this gift of "the word of wisdom" served this Apostle well as he established and nurtured several congregations and wrote at least thirteen books of the New Testa-ment.
The Word of Knowledge

1 Corinthians 12:8 To another the word of knowledge by the same Spirit. Here a different gift is portrayed. The wording to another implies one may receive the gift of "wisdom" and not receive "knowledge." Also, the con-verse is true. One may have "all knowledge" (1 Corinthians 13:2) and not have "the word of wisdom." However, if the Spirit sees fit, one may have both. The Greek word for "knowledge" is gnosis. This word means "knowl-edge of an especial kind" (The New Analytical Greek Lexicon). Jesus refer-red to it as "the key of knowledge" (Luke 11:52). It is the ability to open something to another, to give them entry or access into that which had pre-viously been closed to them. In Romans 2:20, the Apostle Paul equated "knowledge" with "the truth in the law."

Look at the words of the brethren with whom Jesus communed on the Emmaus road: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?" (Luke 24:32). The "word of knowledge" provides the person who possesses this gift with "the key of knowledge," the ability to open the Scriptures to others so that truths which were previously closed and not visible are opened and clearly seen. The Apostle Paul, as is evident through his great host of writings, had this gift as well (2 Corinthians 1:11).

Let us consider another brother who had this particular gift. Acts 18:24-28 introduces a brother named Apollos. Luke, the beloved physician, said he was "an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures" (Acts 18:24). Once Aquila and Priscilla had "expounded unto him the way of God more per-fectly" (Acts 18:26), it is apparent that he had "the word of knowledge." Acts 18:28 says, "He mightily convinced the Jews ... shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ." From the Apostle Paul's words, it is evident Apollos had a little different gift than Paul. Paul said, "I have planted [that is the work of an apostle], Apollos watered" (1 Corinthians 3:6]. Apollos was the one who cultivated and nurtured the seed.

What office does this "word of knowledge" correlate with? Teaching. Ephesians 4:11 says, "He gave some ... teachers." Also, "God hath set some in the church ... thirdly teachers" (1 Corinthians 12:28). Romans 12:7 speaks of "he that teacheth." Apollos, being "mighty in the scriptures," had this gift of knowledge. The Holy Spirit matches the gift with the ministry and the mis-sion that is given to its possessor. In the New Testament, Apollos was such a renowned teacher that he was spoken of and associated with the Apostles Paul and Peter (1 Corinthians 1:12; 3:5-6; 4:6). One noted scholar said this about the importance of teaching: "The message of Christ needs not only
proclaimed; it needs to be explained. Exhortation and invitation without a background of teaching are empty things."

Martin Luther and a number of scholars have attributed the writing of the Book of Hebrews to Apollos. Whether or not this be true, he apparently had this gift, and it served as a special benefit to the New Testament church. In this time of evening light with the "little book open" (Revelation 10:2), the Lord desires to impart much more knowledge. Daniel prophesied of our day and said "knowledge shall be increased" (Daniel 12:4). This gift is very vital to the successful operation of the church today.
JUST A THOUGHT
One must KNOW before they are able to SHOW.

memoryVerses.text: MEMORY VERSE: Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding. —Proverbs 4:7

narrationUnits.text: Beginning with this lesson, we want to examine two particular gifts spe-cifically mentioned in the New Testament.
In our text, as well as in Romans 12:6-8, the Apostle Paul enumerated specific spiritual gifts.
In these listings, the divine penman was certainly not implying the list is exhaustive or entire.
Certainly, these gifts are central and crucial to the successful operation of the New Testament church.
However, it is also evident these passages are not all-inclusive of all gifts.
The psalmist prophesied in Psalm 87:7, "The singers [and] ... the players on instruments shall be there."
There are indeed those who are especially gifted to be one of "the singers" or "the players."
In the Parable of the Talents, we read the gifts are distributed "according to his several ability" (Matthew 25:15).
This verse says, "And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one."
Thus, the apportion-ment rests with the divine, and some may receive "several" gifts.
These gifts possessed by various members of the body of Christ are for a twofold pur-pose: "mak[ing] increase of the body" and "the edifying of itself" (Ephesians 4:16).
As we view the specific gifts mentioned in the Pauline epistles, we also want to see how they were practically performed by the morning-time breth-ren who held various offices.
1 Corinthians 12:8 For to one is given by the Spirit the word of wis-dom.
We must be reminded that these gifts are given.
We are not talking about natural abilities, inclinations, or propensities, but we are talking about "gifts."
In the beginning of the Gospel Day, the ministry had a number of what was termed "unlearned and ignorant men" (Acts 4:13).
The average high school graduate today is probably much better educated than many of the initial morning-time ministers.
Yet, they "turned the world upside down" (Acts 17:6).
Verse 8 speaks of the word of wisdom.
The Greek word for "wisdom" is sophia.
It means "the insight into the true nature of things."
The ancient church father, Clement of Alexandria, said it is "the knowledge of things both human and divine and of their cause."
Sophia is the ultimate understanding and insight into matters both human and divine that can only come from a di-vine source.
It enables us to understand beyond the realm of human compre-hension and to perceive realities as they are in the spiritual and eternal scheme.
It enables the possessor of this ability or gift to act accordingly.
Solomon prayed for sophia: "Give me now wisdom [sophia]" (2 Chron-icles 1:10).
Daniel and the three Hebrew children had this wisdom as well: "God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom" (Daniel 1:17).
This particular attribute is crying for men to seek it: "Doth not wis-dom cry? and understanding put forth her voice?" (Proverbs 8:1).
The wise man admonished us, "Get wisdom, get understanding" (Proverbs 4:5).
Let us view this gift in its New Testament setting.
When the first deacons were selected in the New Testament, the qualifications were: "men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom" (Acts 6:3).
Wisdom is a vital gift to the successful operation of the church.
When Stephen, one of the seven deacons, disputed with the Jews, "they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake" (Acts 6:10).
The Apostle Paul said he was "a wise masterbuilder" (1 Corinthians 3:10).
The wise man said, "Wisdom hath builded her house" (Proverbs 9:1).
We know this "house" is the church (Hebrews 3:6; 1 Timothy 3:15).
The Apostle Paul was successful because he had the gift of wisdom.

This was ev-ident in how he turned the Pharisees and Sadducees against each other and diverted their attention away from him (Acts 23:6-10) and in how he admin-istered church discipline (1 Corinthians 5:13; 2 Corinthians 2:6-8).

Wisdom is an essential gift necessary to fill the office of an apostle or to sow new congregations.
Certainly, this gift of "the word of wisdom" served this Apostle well as he established and nurtured several congregations and wrote at least thirteen books of the New Testa-ment.

Here a different gift is portrayed.
The wording to another implies one may receive the gift of "wisdom" and not receive "knowledge."
Also, the con-verse is true.

blocks.text: LESSON 4
FAITH, HEALING, AND MIRACLES
Scripture Text: 1 Corinthians 12:1-10
DAILY READINGS
☐ Monday: Mark 16:15-20 ☐ Tuesday: Matthew 10:1, 8; 1 Corinthians 12:9-10 ☐ Wednesday: Acts 3:1-11 ☐ Thursday: Acts 19:10-12; Acts 20:7-12 ☐ Friday: Acts 9:36-43 ☐ Saturday: Acts 8:4-7; Acts 21:8
MEMORY VERSE: And they went forth, and preached every where, the Lord working with them, and confirming the word with signs following. —Mark 16:20

In this lesson, we will deviate from studying two gifts and mainly examine the three gifts listed in 1 Corinthians 12:9-10. These gifts are interrelated and are to be functional in the New Testament church for a specific purpose. In Mark 16:17, Jesus said, "These signs shall follow them that believe." One sign was, "They shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover" (Mark 16:18). Then, verse 20 says, "They went forth, and preached every where, the Lord working with them, and confirming the word with signs following." The Emphatic Greek Diaglott renders it as "ratifying the WORD through the ACCOMPANYING Signs."

These particular gifts—faith, healing, and miracles—are specifically in-corporated into the plan of God to serve as confirmation, or ratification, of both the truth that is being heralded and the validity of those who are herald-ing it. This is one reason the enemy, through false religion, has seized upon these particular gifts to make a demonstration to the public; it is their at-tempt to claim legitimacy. In this lesson, we will examine these gifts and the place they are ordained to fill in the furtherance of the Gospel.

1 Corinthians 12:9 To another (is given) faith by the same Spirit. In the apportioning of the spiritual gifts, this particular faith spoken of in this text is a gift. This is not something every child of God is given. Yes, every child of God is "saved through faith" (Ephesians 2:8). We know when the Holy Spirit makes His advent into the heart of a new convert, one attribute He brings as part of "the fruit of the Spirit" is "faith" (Galatians 5:22). Also,

we know every saint has faith because we could not endure "the trying of your faith" (James 1:3) without possessing it. However, the language of our text is clear—this faith is not something everyone possesses. It is speaking of a gift of faith.

An example of this gift is found in the first Christian martyr, Stephen, "a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost" (Acts 6:5).From the description, clearly Stephen's faith was especially notable; he had a special gift of faith. The account in Acts continues, "And Stephen, full of faith and power, did great wonders and miracles among the people" (Acts 6:8). James 2:20 says, "Faith without works is dead." Many times, the gift of faith works in con-junction with the gifts of healing (verse 9) and the working of miracles (verse 10).

James 2:22 instructs, "By works was faith made perfect" (the Greek trans-lation says "complete"). Those who have this gift have a completely oper-ational faith that can be seen in the works of healings and miracles. These three gifts are especially used in apostolic work, in establishing the validity of the claims of the Gospel, and in preparing an unbelieving people to hear the Gospel. These gifts take the Gospel from a purely spiritual realm to a natural realm that the unregenerate may behold. It is a confirmation of the truth of the Gospel. Men may debate doctrine, argue theology, and perhaps even question your testimony, but Acts 4:14 tells us, "Beholding the man which was healed standing with them, they could say nothing against it."
Healing

1 Corinthians 12:9 To another the gifts of healing by the same Spirit. This expression is unique in the sense that gifts is spoken of in the plural tense. Everywhere this is mentioned, it is spoken of in this manner. First Co-rinthians 12:28 speaks of "gifts of healings," and in 1 Corinthians 12:30 the Apostle asked, "Have all the gifts of healing?" Why is it spoken of in this manner? The Emphatic Greek Diaglott renders this phrase as "Gifts of Cures." In Matthew 10:1, when Jesus initially commissioned the twelve, we read, "He gave them power against unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal all manner of sickness and all manner of disease." It takes a different cure to heal disease than to heal just sickness and a different cure, yet, to heal those vexed by unclean spirits. Each different cure is actually a different gracious gift.

1 Corinthians 12:10 Miracles ... discerning of spirits ... kinds of tongues are all spoken of in the plural. Needless to say, there are different spirits and different languages, and certainly, no two miracles are exactly the
same. So it is with healing. Each healing spoken of in our text is the operation of a unique gift fitted for the occasion or circumstance for which it is to be manifested.

In Acts 3:1-11 is the account of the lame man at the gate Beautiful. No-tice specifically the Apostle Peter's words: "Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee" (verse 6). He did not say "such as John and I have." Why? John had a different gift. Peter had the "gifts of healing." It is worthy of mention that Peter did not pray over the lame man nor anoint him with oil. Those are Biblical practices the elders as a whole are instructed to engage in for healing (James 5:14), but Peter was operating a special gift or ability.

Another "manifestation of the Spirit" is recorded in Acts 5:15. It says, "Insomuch that they brought forth the sick into the streets, and laid them on beds and couches, that at the least the shadow of Peter passing by might overshadow some of them." Verse 16 says, "There came also a multitude out of the cities round about ... bringing sick folks ... and they were healed every one." This was another gracious gift; this was not the normal course of heal-ing. It was a special gift. One scholar renders the phrase in 1 Corinthians 12:9 as "the special gifts of healing."
Miracles

1 Corinthians 12:10 To another the working of miracles. The Greek word in this text is dunamis and means "power, a supernatural power." The Apostle Paul had this gift, as evidenced in Acts 19:11-12: "And God wrought special miracles by the hands of Paul: So that from his body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs or aprons, and the diseases departed from them." We also see this in Acts 20:9-12, where a young man "fell down from the third loft, and was taken up dead. And Paul went down, and fell on him, and embracing him said, ... his life is in him."

The Apostle Peter had this gift as well, as we see in the raising of Tabi-tha, or Dorcas, from the dead (Acts 9:36-42). These gifts were especially beneficial to those with the calling to the office of an apostle. An apostle is going into virgin areas and sowing the seed of the Gospel and attempting to raise up new works. The manifestation of these gifts—faith, healing, and miracles—serves as a confirmation of the Word they preach. Consider the raising of Dorcas. Acts 9:42 tells us, "And it was known throughout all Jop-pa; and many believed in the Lord."
It is also beneficial to an evangelist. Acts 8:6 tells us, "And the people with one accord gave heed unto those things which Philip spake, hearing and

seeing the miracles which he did." Acts 21:8 speaks of "Philip the evange-list." The operation of these gifts as a "manifestation of the Spirit" enables the unregenerate, unsaved, and even sectarians (who rest on human senses rather than the divine) to see the truth on a visible level and be convinced of its veracity.

With a religious society about us steeped in humanism and unbelief, may God help us to "covet earnestly the best gifts" (1 Corinthians 12:31), gifts that can be used in the face of an unbelieving world to help sow the truth in new localities and enable honest hearts to see where the truth is and where they may assemble.
JUST A THOUGHT
Men can perform treatments, but Christ performs cures.

narrationUnits.text: In this lesson, we will deviate from studying two gifts and mainly examine the three gifts listed in 1 Corinthians 12:9-10.
These gifts are interrelated and are to be functional in the New Testament church for a specific purpose.
In Mark 16:17, Jesus said, "These signs shall follow them that believe."
One sign was, "They shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover" (Mark 16:18).
Then, verse 20 says, "They went forth, and preached every where, the Lord working with them, and confirming the word with signs following."
The Emphatic Greek Diaglott renders it as "ratifying the WORD through the ACCOMPANYING Signs."

These particular gifts—faith, healing, and miracles—are specifically in-corporated into the plan of God to serve as confirmation, or ratification, of both the truth that is being heralded and the validity of those who are herald-ing it.

This is not something every child of God is given.

We know when the Holy Spirit makes His advent into the heart of a new convert, one attribute He brings as part of "the fruit of the Spirit" is "faith" (Galatians 5:22).

It is speaking of a gift of faith.

The account in Acts continues, "And Stephen, full of faith and power, did great wonders and miracles among the people" (Acts 6:8).
James 2:20 says, "Faith without works is dead."
Many times, the gift of faith works in con-junction with the gifts of healing (verse 9) and the working of miracles (verse 10).
James 2:22 instructs, "By works was faith made perfect" (the Greek trans-lation says "complete").
Those who have this gift have a completely oper-ational faith that can be seen in the works of healings and miracles.
These three gifts are especially used in apostolic work, in establishing the validity of the claims of the Gospel, and in preparing an unbelieving people to hear the Gospel.
These gifts take the Gospel from a purely spiritual realm to a natural realm that the unregenerate may behold.
It is a confirmation of the truth of the Gospel.

blocks.text: LESSON 5
PROPHECY AND PROPHETS
Scripture Texts: 1 Corinthians 12:10
DAILY READINGS

☐ Monday: Romans 12:6; Deuteronomy 18:19-22 ☐ Tuesday: Acts 11:27-28; Acts 21:9-11 ☐ Wednesday: 2 Thessalonians 2:1-12; 1 Timothy 4:1-5 ☐ Thursday: 2 Timothy 3:1-7 ☐ Friday: 1 John 2:18-19; 1 John 4:1-3 ☐ Saturday: Acts 11:27; Acts 13:1; Acts 15:32
MEMORY VERSE: Now there were in the church that was at Antioch certain prophets and teachers. —Acts 13:1

In this lesson, we will consider the gift of prophecy and the correspond-ing office of the New Testament prophet. In addition to our text, we find this gift spoken of in Romans 12:6, which states, "Having then gifts differing ac-cording to the grace that is given to us, whether prophecy, let us prophesy." Then, we see the corresponding office of one who has this gift (1 Corinthians 12:28-29). Ephesians 4:11 relates it as, "He gave some ... prophets."

The realms of modern religion are quick to say prophecy is an Old Testa-ment office, now obsolete or antiquated, but in Ephesians 4:11, it is em-ployed in the same verse as "evangelists," "pastors," and "teachers." If the office of prophet is obsolete or relegated merely to the first century, to be consistent, should not the other offices be obsolete as well? In truth, "the gifts and calling of God are without repentance" (Romans 11:29). Each of the offices (and the gifts necessary to fill them) are New Testament offices, which are to be filled by Him that "might fill all things" (Ephesians 4:10).

Conversely, there is a rise in false religion of some declaring themselves to be "prophets," but Deuteronomy 18:22 tells us, "If the thing follow not, nor come to pass," we will know "the LORD hath not spoken." Also, 2 John 10 admonishes, "If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, re-ceive him not." So, we must be discerning.

1 Corinthians 12:10 To another prophecy. What is prophecy? This term is broader than commonly realized. Prophecy involves two aspects: (1) a foretelling of things to occur, and (2) a forth-telling (defined by The New Analytical Greek Lexicon as "a gifted faculty of setting forth and enforcing revealed truth ... matter of divine teaching set forth by special gift").
The First Aspect of Prophecy—Foretelling

Acts 21:10 mentions "a certain prophet, named Agabus." He was a New Testament prophet. Was this a gift or a "manifestation of the Spirit" (1 Co-rinthians 12:7)? Agabus prophesied to Paul, "Thus saith the Holy Ghost, So shall the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man that owneth this girdle" (Acts 21:11). This was a foretelling. Agabus was the same prophet who "signified by the spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world" (Acts 11:28). Verse 27 uses the term prophets in the plural: "And in these days came prophets from Jerusalem unto Antioch." It is evident that this office is a New Testament office, one utilized by the Spirit and filled by several in-dividuals.

Philip the evangelist had four daughters who prophesied (Acts 21:8-9). Clearly, this was a frequent and functional gift in the New Testament church. The Apostle Paul had this ability as well. In 2 Thessalonians 2:3, he proph-esied, "Let no man deceive you by any means: for that day shall not come, except there come a falling away first." In 1 Timothy 4:1, he proclaimed, "Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith." In 2 Timothy 3:1, he said, "This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come." Here the Apostle Paul was foretelling.
The Second Aspect of Prophecy—Forth-telling

There are those who receive prophecy, and there are those who understand prophecy and expound it. Many times, the gift incorporates both, as in the case of John. John received "the words of the prophecy of this book" (Revela-tion 22:18), but he also had an ability to expound on other prophecies. Con-sider his words in 1 John 2:18, which says, "As ye have heard that antichrist shall come [that term is not employed in the Revelation; he was expounding on other prophecy], even now are there many antichrists; whereby we know that it is the last time." The word prophecy in our text is the Greek word propheteia. It comes from pro (which means "forth") and phemi (which means "to speak"). Vine's Expository Dictionary of New Testament Words says it means: "Speaking forth of the mind and counsel of God. It is the declaration of that which cannot be known by natural means."

In Revelation 10:11, John was told he would eventually leave the confine-ment on Patmos and "prophesy again before many peoples, and nations, and tongues, and kings." It is evident John had the gift of prophecy and filled the office of a prophet. In Revelation 22:9, John was told by the messenger of the Revelation, "I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren the prophets."
John was numbered among the brethren who were prophets.

In today's religious confusion concerning prophecy and Revelation, proph-ecy is a vital gift, not only to foretell what lies ahead, but to forth-tell the previous prophecies and revelation truths that have brought the people of God to the present-day position. The Lord desires His people to understand prophetic truths. Prophecy is to edify and instruct the church, not "them that believe not" (1 Corinthians 14:22; 14:4).

The Lord desires prophetic truths be forth-told to give a historical bearing of what has occurred through the Gospel Day, of where we are, and of how we arrived where we are today. God also desires the New Testament church to have prophets who can tell where we are going and what yet lies ahead in the prophetic spectrum.
Prophets—Also New Testament Office

The office of prophets was no small, unimportant office in the New Testa-ment church. It is mentioned frequently (and in the plural) in the Book of Acts. Acts 11:27 says, "And in these days came prophets [plural] from Jeru-salem unto Antioch." Acts 13:1 tells us, "Now there were in the church that was at Antioch certain prophets [plural] and teachers; as Barnabas, and Simeon that was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen ... and Saul." These offices of "prophets and teachers" were fully functional in the early morning-time New Testament church.

Acts 15:32 reads, "And Judas and Silas, being prophets also themselves, exhorted the brethren with many words, and confirmed them." In 1 Corin-thians 14:37, the Apostle Paul said, "If any man think himself to be a prophet ...." This was clearly an accepted and functional gift and office in the first century. It is just as vitally needed in this twenty-first century. Let us not embrace the false thinking of sectarianism that this gift is obsolete.

All the gifts are "to profit withal" (1 Corinthians 12:7). Without the oper-ation of each Biblical gift, the body will experience a deficiency. All "are necessary" (1 Corinthians 12:22). If ever the saints who are scattered abroad needed the prophetic truths heralded to expose the falsities of sectarianism so that they can come leaping and shouting home to Zion, it is today. If ever the church needed enlightenment on what lies before her and how to achieve her task, it is today. The Apostle placed great importance on this gift when he said, "Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts, but rather that ye may prophesy" (1 Corinthians 14:1). God help us to "covet earnestly" (1 Co-rinthians 12:31) these gifts so that the church may benefit.
JUST A THOUGHT
The gifts are "to profit withal," but to gain the "profit," we must be with all!

narrationUnits.text: In this lesson, we will consider the gift of prophecy and the correspond-ing office of the New Testament prophet.
In addition to our text, we find this gift spoken of in Romans 12:6, which states, "Having then gifts differing ac-cording to the grace that is given to us, whether prophecy, let us prophesy."
Then, we see the corresponding office of one who has this gift (1 Corinthians 12:28-29).
Ephesians 4:11 relates it as, "He gave some ... prophets."

The realms of modern religion are quick to say prophecy is an Old Testa-ment office, now obsolete or antiquated, but in Ephesians 4:11, it is em-ployed in the same verse as "evangelists," "pastors," and "teachers."
If the office of prophet is obsolete or relegated merely to the first century, to be consistent, should not the other offices be obsolete as well?
In truth, "the gifts and calling of God are without repentance" (Romans 11:29).
Each of the offices (and the gifts necessary to fill them) are New Testament offices, which are to be filled by Him that "might fill all things" (Ephesians 4:10).

Conversely, there is a rise in false religion of some declaring themselves to be "prophets," but Deuteronomy 18:22 tells us, "If the thing follow not, nor come to pass," we will know "the LORD hath not spoken."
Also, 2 John 10 admonishes, "If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, re-ceive him not."
So, we must be discerning.
1 Corinthians 12:10 To another prophecy.
What is prophecy?
This term is broader than commonly realized.

Prophecy involves two aspects: (1) a foretelling of things to occur, and (2) a forth-telling (defined by The New Analytical Greek Lexicon as "a gifted faculty of setting forth and enforcing revealed truth ... matter of divine teaching set forth by special gift").
Acts 21:10 mentions "a certain prophet, named Agabus."
He was a New Testament prophet.
Was this a gift or a "manifestation of the Spirit" (1 Co-rinthians 12:7)?
Agabus prophesied to Paul, "Thus saith the Holy Ghost, So shall the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man that owneth this girdle" (Acts 21:11).
This was a foretelling.
Agabus was the same prophet who "signified by the spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world" (Acts 11:28).
Verse 27 uses the term prophets in the plural: "And in these days came prophets from Jerusalem unto Antioch."
It is evident that this office is a New Testament office, one utilized by the Spirit and filled by several in-dividuals.
Philip the evangelist had four daughters who prophesied (Acts 21:8-9).
Clearly, this was a frequent and functional gift in the New Testament church.
The Apostle Paul had this ability as well.
In 2 Thessalonians 2:3, he proph-esied, "Let no man deceive you by any means: for that day shall not come, except there come a falling away first."
In 1 Timothy 4:1, he proclaimed, "Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith."
In 2 Timothy 3:1, he said, "This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come."
Here the Apostle Paul was foretelling.
There are those who receive prophecy, and there are those who understand prophecy and expound it.
Many times, the gift incorporates both, as in the case of John.
John received "the words of the prophecy of this book" (Revela-tion 22:18), but he also had an ability to expound on other prophecies.

Con-sider his words in 1 John 2:18, which says, "As ye have heard that antichrist shall come [that term is not employed in the Revelation; he was expounding on other prophecy], even now are there many antichrists; whereby we know that it is the last time."
The word prophecy in our text is the Greek word propheteia.
It comes from pro (which means "forth") and phemi (which means "to speak").
Vine's Expository Dictionary of New Testament Words says it means: "Speaking forth of the mind and counsel of God.
It is the declaration of that which cannot be known by natural means."

It is evident John had the gift of prophecy and filled the office of a prophet.

John was numbered among the brethren who were prophets.

The Lord desires His people to understand prophetic truths.
Prophecy is to edify and instruct the church, not "them that believe not" (1 Corinthians 14:22; 14:4).
The Lord desires prophetic truths be forth-told to give a historical bearing of what has occurred through the Gospel Day, of where we are, and of how we arrived where we are today.

blocks.text: LESSON 6
DISCERNMENT AND MERCY
Scripture Texts: Romans 12:8; 1 Corinthians 12:10
DAILY READINGS

☐ Monday: Jude 3; 1 Corinthians 10:13; Malachi 3:16-18 ☐ Tuesday: 1 Corinthians 2:14-16 ☐ Wednesday: Acts 5:1-10; Ecclesiastes 10:20 ☐ Thursday: Acts 8:18-24; Acts 11:19-26 ☐ Friday: Acts 15:36-41; Colossians 4:10; 1 Timothy 4:11 ☐ Saturday: 1 Corinthians 5:1-5; 2 Corinthians 2:6-8
MEMORY VERSE: Then shall ye return, and discern between the righteous and the wicked, between him that serveth God and him that serveth him not. —Malachi 3:18

In this lesson, we will consider two gifts that complement each other. These gifts operate closely together, for it is necessary to have the one in or-der to properly know when to dispense the other. Our text in the Corinthian letter speaks of discerning of spirits, and in the Roman Epistle, a gift of mercy is mentioned. It is rather astounding that mercy would be listed as a specific gift.

Romans 12:8 He that showeth mercy [let him do it], with cheerfulness. Rarely do we think of showing mercy as a gift, but from its inclusion in this listing, it evidently is so. These two gifts have a correlation. Without discern-ment, how can it be known whether a situation warrants judgment or mercy? In a day of a specious apostasy, these two Biblical gifts are as needful to the successful operation of the church today as they were in the first century.
A Common Salvation

Jude 3 speaks of our "common salvation," and there are several attributes "common," or universal, to all who possess this experience of salvation. The most familiar is that we all share "temptation ... such as is common to man" (1 Corinthians 10:13). There are other aspects of commonality as well. The Prophet Malachi spoke of this New Testament dispensation, declaring: "In that day [a prophetic expression of this Gospel Day] when I make up my jewels .... Then shall ye return, and discern between the righteous and the

wicked, between him that serveth God and him that serveth him not" (Mala-chi 3:17-18). This prophetic passage reveals each of the "jewels," or saints, have a certain amount of discernment; it is common to all.

In 1 Corinthians 2:15, we are told, "But he that is spiritual judgeth ['dis-cerneth'] all things." Every spiritual person has a certain amount of discern-ment. We are each enjoined, "Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful" (Luke 6:36). But in this lesson's text, we see more depicted than just the common dispensation of these abilities; we see specific gifts.
What Is Discernment?

1 Corinthians 12:10 To another discerning of spirits. Incorporating the words "to another" indicates not everyone receives this specific gift of discer-nment. What is this gift of discernment? First Corinthians 2:15 gives insight, saying, "He that is spiritual judgeth all things." The Greek word for "judg-eth" is anakrino and means "the exercise of a discerning judgment of all things as to their true value" (Vine's Expository Dictionary of New Testa-ment Words). It is the same word used in reference to trying one judicially ("examined," Acts 28:18; "examine," 1 Corinthians 9:3). It is the ability, through "the manifestation of the Spirit" (1 Corinthians 12:7), of judging be-tween that which is of the Holy Spirit and that which is prompted or promo-ted by another spirit. It is judging between that which is divine and that which is diabolical. One rendering of 1 Corinthians 12:10 describes it as "the ability to distinguish between different kinds of spirits."
Examples of the Gift of Discernment

Let us consider Biblical accounts where this gift was in operation. In Acts 5:1-10, the account of Ananias and Sapphira is recorded. When they "kept back part of the price," the only ones "privy to it" (verse 2) were Ananias and his wife, Sapphira. Yet, when Ananias came before Peter, Peter said, "Anan-ias, why hath Satan filled thine heart to lie to the Holy Ghost, and to keep back part of the price of the land?" (verse 3). How did Peter know that? Ec-clesiastes 10:20 says, "A bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which hath wings shall tell the matter." That "bird" is symbolic of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 3:16); the gift of discernment, given by the Holy Spirit, revealed the matter to Peter.

Look at when the Gospel was introduced to Samaria. Acts 8:13-14 says: "Then Simon himself believed also: and when he was baptized, he continued with Philip [notice Philip's call was as an 'evangelist'; Acts 21:8].... Now

when the apostles [those responsible and gifted to start new works] which were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent unto them Peter and John." To understand why Peter was selected, look at what occurred in verses 21-23. Peter discerned Simon's spirit, saying in verse 23, "I perceive that thou art in the gall of bitterness, and in the bond of iniquity."

Peter was sent because he had the gift of discernment. Certainly the Lord used Philip the evangelist greatly in Samaria, but there were limitations to his abilities, and there was a place where other members of the body needed to operate their gifts and fill their offices. Another manifestation of discern-ment is seen in Paul's rebuke of the "damsel possessed with a spirit of divina-tion" (Acts 16:16). In this passage (Acts 16:16-18), the damsel spoke the truth, but the spirit she possessed was discerned by Paul to be devilish. This is a very necessary and important gift in the field of apostolic work. When he goes into a new area, he does not have the time to learn or to get to know the people as well perhaps as a pastor would. He needs to be able to discern what he is dealing with so that he can operate appropriately.
Discernment With Mercy

Thus far, we have seen discernment operate in a manner that required re-buke and judgment to be meted out, but there is another aspect to discern-ment. In Acts 11:19-26, the Gospel was first purposely introduced to the Gentiles in Antioch. When "tidings of these things came unto the ears of the church which was in Jerusalem: ... they sent forth Barnabas" (verse 22). But when Barnabas "came, and had seen the grace of God" (verse 23), look at what he did. "Then departed Barnabas to Tarsus, for to seek Saul" (verse 25). Why? In Romans 11:13, Paul called himself "the apostle of the Gen-tiles." In Antioch, the first Gentile congregation was established, and Barna-bas discerned Paul's call to the Gentiles.

Consider the young man "John, whose surname was Mark" (Acts 15:37), who traveled along on the first missionary trip taken by Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:2). "John departing from them returned to Jerusalem" (Acts 13:13). Thus, when they were ready to take their second journey: "Barnabas deter-mined to take with them John, whose surname was Mark. But Paul thought not good to take him with them, who departed from them from Pamphylia, and went not with them to the work" (Acts 15:37-38). Here we see discern-ment working in conjunction with "he that sheweth mercy" (Romans 12:8).
John Mark, who later wrote the Gospel of Mark, was Barnabas' nephew (Colossians 4:10). No doubt, he may have known him better than Paul, but

Barnabas also discerned something in John Mark that others did not see at that juncture (just as he earlier discerned a special ability in Paul). Barnabas felt it warranted mercy rather than judgment. The brethren recognized he had this gift, for in Acts 4:36, he was "surnamed Barnabas, (which is, being in-terpreted, The son of consolation)." Later, the Apostle Paul saw merit in John Mark as well. Speaking of Mark in 2 Timothy 4:11, Paul said, "He is profitable to me for the ministry," and he instructed the Colossians, "If he come unto you, receive him" (Colossians 4:10).

If not for Barnabas' discernment and gift of showing "mercy, with cheer-fulness" (Romans 12:8), this tender plant would have been crushed in its growth and could never have developed into the stalwart leader that John Mark became. There is a time for judgment and a time for mercy; discern-ment distinguishes between these seasons. In 1 Corinthians 5:1-5, Paul ad-monished that severe judgment be put on one who had his father's wife, but in 2 Corinthians 2:6, he discerned, "Sufficient to such a man is this punish-ment." He added, "Confirm your love toward him" (verse 8).

This vital gift can help a pastor know how to administer discipline. It can aid pastors or teachers in recognizing those coming up under them whom the Lord has His hand on. Properly exercised, this gift can reveal the devious "Simon the Sorcerers" trying to work among us and put the proper judgment on them. Additionally, if it is working as it ought, it can also recognize the Apostle Pauls and John Marks whom the Lord would like to raise from ob-scurity to the leadership of the church.
JUST A THOUGHT
Discernment can see a diamond in the rough. Mercy works with the rough to secure the diamond.

memoryVerses.text: MEMORY VERSE: Then shall ye return, and discern between the righteous and the wicked, between him that serveth God and him that serveth him not. —Malachi 3:18

narrationUnits.text: In this lesson, we will consider two gifts that complement each other.
These gifts operate closely together, for it is necessary to have the one in or-der to properly know when to dispense the other.
Our text in the Corinthian letter speaks of discerning of spirits, and in the Roman Epistle, a gift of mercy is mentioned.
It is rather astounding that mercy would be listed as a specific gift.
Romans 12:8 He that showeth mercy [let him do it], with cheerfulness.
Rarely do we think of showing mercy as a gift, but from its inclusion in this listing, it evidently is so.
These two gifts have a correlation.
Without discern-ment, how can it be known whether a situation warrants judgment or mercy?
In a day of a specious apostasy, these two Biblical gifts are as needful to the successful operation of the church today as they were in the first century.
Jude 3 speaks of our "common salvation," and there are several attributes "common," or universal, to all who possess this experience of salvation.
The most familiar is that we all share "temptation ... such as is common to man" (1 Corinthians 10:13).
There are other aspects of commonality as well.
The Prophet Malachi spoke of this New Testament dispensation, declaring: "In that day [a prophetic expression of this Gospel Day] when I make up my jewels ....
Then shall ye return, and discern between the righteous and the wicked, between him that serveth God and him that serveth him not" (Mala-chi 3:17-18).
This prophetic passage reveals each of the "jewels," or saints, have a certain amount of discernment; it is common to all.
In 1 Corinthians 2:15, we are told, "But he that is spiritual judgeth ['dis-cerneth'] all things."
Every spiritual person has a certain amount of discern-ment.
We are each enjoined, "Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful" (Luke 6:36).
But in this lesson's text, we see more depicted than just the common dispensation of these abilities; we see specific gifts.
1 Corinthians 12:10 To another discerning of spirits.
Incorporating the words "to another" indicates not everyone receives this specific gift of discer-nment.
What is this gift of discernment?
First Corinthians 2:15 gives insight, saying, "He that is spiritual judgeth all things."
The Greek word for "judg-eth" is anakrino and means "the exercise of a discerning judgment of all things as to their true value" (Vine's Expository Dictionary of New Testa-ment Words).
It is the same word used in reference to trying one judicially ("examined," Acts 28:18; "examine," 1 Corinthians 9:3).
It is the ability, through "the manifestation of the Spirit" (1 Corinthians 12:7), of judging be-tween that which is of the Holy Spirit and that which is prompted or promo-ted by another spirit.
It is judging between that which is divine and that which is diabolical.
One rendering of 1 Corinthians 12:10 describes it as "the ability to distinguish between different kinds of spirits."
Let us consider Biblical accounts where this gift was in operation.
In Acts 5:1-10, the account of Ananias and Sapphira is recorded.
When they "kept back part of the price," the only ones "privy to it" (verse 2) were Ananias and his wife, Sapphira.
Yet, when Ananias came before Peter, Peter said, "Anan-ias, why hath Satan filled thine heart to lie to the Holy Ghost, and to keep back part of the price of the land?" (verse 3).
How did Peter know that?
Ec-clesiastes 10:20 says, "A bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which hath wings shall tell the matter."
That "bird" is symbolic of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 3:16); the gift of discernment, given by the Holy Spirit, revealed the matter to Peter.
Look at when the Gospel was introduced to Samaria.
Acts 8:13-14 says: "Then Simon himself believed also: and when he was baptized, he continued with Philip [notice Philip's call was as an 'evangelist'; Acts 21:8]....
Now when the apostles [those responsible and gifted to start new works] which were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent unto them Peter and John."
To understand why Peter was selected, look at what occurred in verses 21-23.
Peter discerned Simon's spirit, saying in verse 23, "I perceive that thou art in the gall of bitterness, and in the bond of iniquity."
Peter was sent because he had the gift of discernment.

Certainly the Lord used Philip the evangelist greatly in Samaria, but there were limitations to his abilities, and there was a place where other members of the body needed to operate their gifts and fill their offices.
Another manifestation of discern-ment is seen in Paul's rebuke of the "damsel possessed with a spirit of divina-tion" (Acts 16:16).
In this passage (Acts 16:16-18), the damsel spoke the truth, but the spirit she possessed was discerned by Paul to be devilish.
This is a very necessary and important gift in the field of apostolic work.
When he goes into a new area, he does not have the time to learn or to get to know the people as well perhaps as a pastor would.
He needs to be able to discern what he is dealing with so that he can operate appropriately.
Thus far, we have seen discernment operate in a manner that required re-buke and judgment to be meted out, but there is another aspect to discern-ment.
In Acts 11:19-26, the Gospel was first purposely introduced to the Gentiles in Antioch.
When "tidings of these things came unto the ears of the church which was in Jerusalem: ... they sent forth Barnabas" (verse 22).
But when Barnabas "came, and had seen the grace of God" (verse 23), look at what he did. "Then departed Barnabas to Tarsus, for to seek Saul" (verse 25).
Why?
In Romans 11:13, Paul called himself "the apostle of the Gen-tiles."
In Antioch, the first Gentile congregation was established, and Barna-bas discerned Paul's call to the Gentiles.

Consider the young man "John, whose surname was Mark" (Acts 15:37), who traveled along on the first missionary trip taken by Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:2). "John departing from them returned to Jerusalem" (Acts 13:13).
Thus, when they were ready to take their second journey: "Barnabas deter-mined to take with them John, whose surname was Mark.
But Paul thought not good to take him with them, who departed from them from Pamphylia, and went not with them to the work" (Acts 15:37-38).
Here we see discern-ment working in conjunction with "he that sheweth mercy" (Romans 12:8).
John Mark, who later wrote the Gospel of Mark, was Barnabas' nephew (Colossians 4:10).
No doubt, he may have known him better than Paul, but Barnabas also discerned something in John Mark that others did not see at that juncture (just as he earlier discerned a special ability in Paul).
Barnabas felt it warranted mercy rather than judgment.
The brethren recognized he had this gift, for in Acts 4:36, he was "surnamed Barnabas, (which is, being in-terpreted, The son of consolation)."
Later, the Apostle Paul saw merit in John Mark as well.
Speaking of Mark in 2 Timothy 4:11, Paul said, "He is profitable to me for the ministry," and he instructed the Colossians, "If he come unto you, receive him" (Colossians 4:10).

If not for Barnabas' discernment and gift of showing "mercy, with cheer-fulness" (Romans 12:8), this tender plant would have been crushed in its growth and could never have developed into the stalwart leader that John Mark became.
There is a time for judgment and a time for mercy; discern-ment distinguishes between these seasons.
In 1 Corinthians 5:1-5, Paul ad-monished that severe judgment be put on one who had his father's wife, but in 2 Corinthians 2:6, he discerned, "Sufficient to such a man is this punish-ment."
He added, "Confirm your love toward him" (verse 8).
This vital gift can help a pastor know how to administer discipline.
It can aid pastors or teachers in recognizing those coming up under them whom the Lord has His hand on.
Properly exercised, this gift can reveal the devious "Simon the Sorcerers" trying to work among us and put the proper judgment on them.
Additionally, if it is working as it ought, it can also recognize the Apostle Pauls and John Marks whom the Lord would like to raise from ob-scurity to the leadership of the church.
Discernment can see a diamond in the rough.
Mercy works with the rough to secure the diamond.

blocks.text: LESSON 7
TONGUES AND INTERPRETATION OF TONGUES
Scripture Text: 1 Corinthians 12:10
DAILY READINGS
☐ Monday: Acts 2:1-38 ☐ Tuesday: Acts 10:44-47; Acts 19:6 ☐ Wednesday: Genesis 11:1-9 ☐ Thursday: 1 Corinthians 14:18-19, 27-28 ☐ Friday: Daniel 5:5-28 ☐ Saturday: Matthew 13:38; Matthew 28:19
MEMORY VERSE: And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born? —Acts 2:8

In this lesson, we will consider the last two gifts mentioned in our text: di-vers kinds of tongues and the interpretation of tongues. These two gifts have been greatly misrepresented and misused in the realms of religion. Modern Pentecostal movements advocate that speaking in tongues is the initial evidence of the Holy Ghost baptism and that this is an evidence that all should receive. However, the writer clearly stated, "All these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will" (1 Corinthians 12:11).

The questions posed in 1 Corinthians 12:30, "Do all speak with tongues? do all interpret?" beg the obvious answer of no. No more than all are apostles or all are prophets, as the question is posed in the preceding verse (verse 29). It was never ordained that all would be recipients of these gifts. This explic-itly teaches that we do not all receive the same gifts. The word "initial" does not appear in the Scriptures, and the only place "evidence" appears in the New Testament is in Hebrews 11:1, which declares, "Faith is ... the evidence of things not seen." Faith is the evidence, not a manifestation of "tongues."
What Are "Divers Kinds of Tongues"?

1 Corinthians 12:10 To another divers kinds of tongues. The sacred writer informed us in his elaboration on "diversities of gifts" (1 Corinthians 12:4) that there is one gift known as divers kinds of tongues. One rendering expresses it: "Still another person is able to speak in languages he never

learned." The word divers in The Expanded Greek Translation of the New Testament is "various." The phrase is offered as "various kinds of lan-guages." The Emphatic Greek Diaglott says "different languages." This gift is not speaking in some unintelligible manner but rather in a language under-stood by the hearer.
Biblical Examples

Scriptures list three explicit occasions where this gift was in operation. The most famous account is the Day of Pentecost, so called because it was a Jewish feast (Feast of Pentecost). The word Pentecost comes from the Greek word pentekoste and literally means "fiftieth." The Feast of Pentecost derived its name because it was fifty days after the Jewish Feast of Passover. Several truths are notable in this account (Acts 2:1-38). Verse 4 says they "began to speak with other tongues" (the Greek word is glossa, which means "languages"), and verse 6 says that "every man heard them speak in his own language." Several truths are here revealed about this gift.

First, the languages they heard were understandable. Verse 11 says, "We do hear them speak in our tongues [or languages] the wonderful works of God." Second, the purpose for the gift is revealed, which was to communi-cate the Gospel. Third, when the spiritual gift of languages is operating, there is no need of interpretation. In each of the three instances where we see this gift operating, these three truths are substantiated (Acts 2:1-38; 10:44-47; 19:6).

In Acts 2:9-11, sixteen distinct localities or ethnic groups are enumerated. In verse 14, we read, "But Peter, standing up with the eleven, lifted up his voice, and said unto them, ... hearken to my words." Then, in verses 15-36, he preached the Gospel. Verse 37 tells us, "Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart." His message was understandable to all sixteen dialects. Yet, Acts 4:13 informs us Peter was "unlearned and ignorant," as far as formal education was concerned. This was the operation of a gift; Pe-ter spoke, and they each heard him "speak in our tongues" (Acts 2:11).

It is important to note that while Paul wrote in 1 Corinthians 14:18, "I speak with tongues more than ye all," there is no scriptural evidence he had the gift of languages. Although one may have gained the ability through edu-cation to speak in different languages, that is not the gift mentioned in our lesson text. It is obvious in the three accounts in Acts that it was the oper-ation of this gift. It is beyond the scope of this study, but it should be men-tioned that the "unknown tongue" spoken of in 1 Corinthians, Chapter 14, has nothing to do with this gift. It refers to the practice that was taking place
in Corinth—ones speaking in a language they knew but was unknown to the hearers.
Why Were Tongues Used?

The three instances where the employment of this gift are listed were historic occasions. Acts, Chapter 2, explains that the truth was introduced to "Jews, devout men" (verse 5); it was introduced to the Jewish nation. In the case at Cornelius' house, it was a confirmation that the new covenant in-corporated "the Gentiles" (Acts 10:45; 11:17-18). The Gospel reached the full spectrum of men when the twelve Samaritan disciples at Ephesus em-braced the message "and prophesied" (Acts 19:1-7), or the Twentieth Cen-tury New Testament says "to preach" (Acts 19:6). (Dr. Lawrence J. Chest-nut, in his book True Bible Tongues, devotes the entirety of Chapter 10 to what he denotes as "the twelve Samaritans at Ephesus.") This gift is to be used to communicate by declaration or acceptance of the Gospel.

In Genesis 11:1-9, when men aspired to build their own way to "reach unto heaven" (verse 4), God said, "Let us go down, and there confound their language, that they may not understand one another's speech" (verse 7). A condition was created where "the LORD scattered them" (verse 8), and "the name of it [was] called Babel ["Confusion"; the Septuagint]" (verse 9). In the three instances we are studying of first century civilization embracing the truth, we see a return to "that which was from the beginning" (1 John 1:1).

Through the Gospel and its acceptance, men from "every nation under heaven" (Acts 2:5) were brought back into unity and able to understand one another by the operation of this spiritual gift. This is why it occurred on three occasions and to three distinct groups: the Jews, the Gentiles, and the Samaritans (a mixed race of Jew and Gentile). These three accounts substan-tiate the truth of Acts 10:35, which reads, "But in every nation he that fear-eth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him."

Yet today, if a language barrier exists and impairs the ability to communi-cate the Gospel, this gift can be a "manifestation of the Spirit" (1 Corinthians 12:7) to enable the speaker to preach in a language previously unknown to him and to communicate the Gospel. It still acts as a confirmation of the Word (Mark 16:17-20).
The Gift of Interpretation
1 Corinthians 12:10 To another the interpretation of tongues. This is another of the spiritual gifts spoken of in this chapter. While 1 Corinthians,

Chapter 14, speaks of an "interpreter" (verse 28) and of "let[ting] one inter-pret" (verse 27), that does not necessarily indicate a spiritual gift. One may be able to interpret a language because of his familiarity with it or because of educational training. The "interpretation" mentioned in our text is a gift. Interpretation in our text is hermeneia in the Greek language and means "translation." Hermeneia comes from the Greek word Hermes, the Greek name of the pagan god Mercury, who was regarded as the messenger of the gods. It denotes "to explain" and is used for explaining the meaning of words in a different language" (Vine's Expository Dictionary of New Testament Words).

Though not a New Testament account, we see an example of interpre-tation in Daniel, Chapter 5. Daniel 5:5 says, "Fingers of a man's hand ... wrote over against the candlestick upon the plaister of the wall." The wise men of Babylon "could not read the writing, nor make known to the king the interpretation" (Daniel 5:8). The ministers in spiritual Babylon still cannot read the Word and understand its message yet today. But Daniel had "an ex-cellent spirit" (Daniel 5:12), and he interpreted the message of truth (Daniel 5:26-28).

The purpose of the New Testament gift of interpretation is to make the truth understandable to the masses when it is sent in a language they do not understand. Today, one may travel to foreign soil to encourage missionary work, be unable to speak their language, and not have the gift of languages. In those cases, the Lord will use those with the gift of interpretation so that God's Word may be understood. These gifts are needed yet today. The field is still the world (Matthew 13:38), and the commission is still, "Go ye into all the world" (Mark 16:15). As long as there are language barriers, there will be a need for the operation of these gifts.
JUST A THOUGHT
The evidence of the Holy Ghost is a holy life!

No more than all are apostles or all are prophets, as the question is posed in the preceding verse (verse 29).
It was never ordained that all would be recipients of these gifts.
This explic-itly teaches that we do not all receive the same gifts.
The word "initial" does not appear in the Scriptures, and the only place "evidence" appears in the New Testament is in Hebrews 11:1, which declares, "Faith is ... the evidence of things not seen."
Faith is the evidence, not a manifestation of "tongues."
1 Corinthians 12:10 To another divers kinds of tongues.
The sacred writer informed us in his elaboration on "diversities of gifts" (1 Corinthians 12:4) that there is one gift known as divers kinds of tongues.
One rendering expresses it: "Still another person is able to speak in languages he never learned."

The phrase is offered as "various kinds of lan-guages."
The Emphatic Greek Diaglott says "different languages."
