lines.text: CHURCH OF GOD
SUNDAY SCHOOL QUARTERLY
GIFTS, OFFICES, AND
THE OPERATION OF THE
NEW TESTAMENT CHURCH
GIFTS, OFFICES, AND THE OPERATION OF
THE NEW TESTAMENT CHURCH
by Earl R. Borders
CONTENTS
Tongues and Interpretation of Tongues. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 24
Desiring Gifts and Every Joint Supplieth . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 48
NOTE TO THE TEACHERS
This booklet is intended to be a help in preparing Sunday school les-
sons. The title, subject, and topics are only the menu. It is your respon-
sibility to prepare the meal.
The proper ingredients are the salty inspirations of the Holy Spirit,
seasoned with His grace. Bake the ingredients at a hot temperature in the
oven of prayer. The time-tested recipe for preparing a nutritious meal is
found in 2 Timothy 2:15, "Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a
workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of
truth."
LESSON 1
AN INTRODUCTION
Scripture Text: Romans 12:3-8
DAILY READINGS
☐ Monday: 2 Kings 2:9-15
☐ Tuesday: 1 Corinthians 12:28-31
☐ Wednesday: Ephesians 4:7-12
☐ Thursday: Romans 12:3-8
☐ Friday: 1 Corinthians 12:1, 7-11
☐ Saturday: Proverbs 25:14; Proverbs 18:16
MEMORY VERSE: But covet earnestly the best gifts.
—1 Corinthians 12:31
I have a dual burden behind this study: (1) to instruct (as "all scripture is
given ... for instruction"; 2 Timothy 3:16), and (2) that through exposure to
these truths, desire might be created within you to "covet earnestly the best
gifts" (1 Corinthians 12:31) so that "a man [might] desire the office" (1 Tim-
othy 3:1). For the truth to be perpetuated until our Lord returns requires the
continual operation of spiritual gifts in the filling of ecclesiastical offices.
The Apostle Paul said in Romans 11:29, "For the gifts and calling of God are
without repentance." The Expanded Greek Translation of the New Testa-
ment renders it, "For the gifts in grace at the calling of God are with respect
to a change of mind irrevocable."
The gifts and offices that led to the successful operation of the primitive
church are just as vitally needed for the church's successful operation today.
As revered leaders step off the stage of action, gifts do not die with them.
Just as Elijah's mantle fell upon Elisha (2 Kings 2:13-15), so God's plan to-
day is to call and prepare successive leadership. However, it is important to
note that Elisha coveted the gift Elijah had (2 Kings 2:9) and desired to fill
his office. God is looking for just such ones today.
Ezekiel 22:30 reads, "And I sought for a man among them." It is our bur-
den, as you study these lessons, that not only will "the eyes of your under-
standing ... [be] enlightened" (Ephesians 1:18) but also that a desire will be
created to "covet earnestly the best gifts" (1 Corinthians 12:31), that we may
see no office deficient or lacking.
Gifts and Offices
Romans 12:6 Having then gifts differing according to the grace that
is given to us. There are different gifts. First Corinthians 12:8-9 says, "To
one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowl-
edge ... To another faith ... to another the gifts of healing" and so forth. Not
all receive the same gifts, and there is a valid reason it is ordained that way.
The gift is the talent or ability that equips one to fill a particular office. It
would be difficult to be called as one of the "teachers" (1 Corinthians 12:28;
Ephesians 4:11) and not have "the word of knowledge" (1 Corinthians 12:8),
or to be "called to be an apostle" (Romans 1:1) without the gift of "faith"
(1 Corinthians 12:9). The gifts equip the persons for the offices the Lord de-
sires they fill.
The Apostle Paul said in Romans 11:13, "I am the apostle of the Gentiles,
I magnify mine office." First Timothy 3:1 declares, "If a man desire the of-
fice of a bishop, he desireth a good work." Ephesians 4:11 gives a listing of
the ministerial offices in the church: "some, apostles; and some, prophets;
and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers." Five offices are
listed. (Some scholars question whether "teachers" is a separate category, but
1 Corinthians 12:28 explains it is a separate office.) Each office is essential.
Without the operation of each of these offices, the church will be deficient
and handicapped, as a body with a missing member.
Romans 12:4 All members have not the same office. The different gifts
are placed in different offices. The church is operated through these offices.
In sectarianism, men who do not have the gifts fill offices, and the results are
tragic. The wise man said, "Whoso boasteth himself of a false gift is like
clouds and wind without rain" (Proverbs 25:14). This is why Babylon is so
dry and parched. Conversely, the Lord does not want a man on whom He be-
stows gifts and talents to hide his "talent in the earth" (Matthew 25:25), but
to be willing so that his "gift maketh room for him" (Proverbs 18:16). This
requires making the personal sacrifice required to step up and fill the office,
or offices, the Lord may be calling him to fill.
Many Members—One Body
Romans 12:4 We have many members in one body. One of the most
famous and frequent analogies the Apostle Paul used regarding the church
is that of a body. The church is one body, but as with the natural body, for
it to function properly requires the operation of many members. There must
ever be a spirit of cooperation among the many members. Each member
must recognize the importance of the role of the others and "should have the
same care one for another" (1 Corinthians 12:25).
We also must recognize that because there are different gifts, the grace
that is given to us (Romans 12:6) is in relation to our gift. We should fill
the office that coincides with our gifts. For example, one may have the gift
to fill the office of an evangelist and have a tremendous ability in that area,
yet lack "the word of wisdom" (1 Corinthians 12:8) necessary to be a suc-
cessful pastor. Much havoc has been brought about over the years by people
not abiding in their calling. Grace is only given for the particular gift that we
possess.
Romans 12:3 Think soberly, according as God hath dealt to every
man the measure of faith. Ephesians 4:7 reads, "But unto every one of us
is given grace according to the measure of the gift of Christ." There is grace
only in proportion to the gift given. When one steps outside the bounds of
that gift, the grace is not operational. Therefore, while it behooves us to
"covet earnestly the best gifts" (1 Corinthians 12:31), we must also have an
understanding of the gifts we possess and abide within their bounds. Those
gifts will prepare us for service in particular offices, but we must be cautious
that neither our zeal causes us to overstep our gifts, nor our hesitance causes
us to fail to step up when the Spirit of God directs.
In this quarterly, we will study what a gift actually is, what it is used for,
and how we are to use it. Also, we will study the various offices that must
be filled for the successful operation of the church. It is my desire that we
study these truths so that each of us will have the keen sense that we truly
need to have "an ear [to] ... hear what the Spirit saith" (Revelation 2:7).
JUST A THOUGHT
He who steps out of the boundary of his gift
leaves himself open for the enemy to sift!
LESSON 2
GIFTS
Scripture Texts: 1 Corinthians 12:1; Ephesians 4:7-8
DAILY READINGS
☐ Monday: 1 Corinthians 1:4-8
☐ Tuesday: Matthew 25:15; 1 Corinthians 12:11
☐ Wednesday: 1 Corinthians 7:7; 1 Peter 4:10-11
☐ Thursday: Ephesians 4:16; 1 Corinthians 7:20
☐ Friday: 1 Corinthians 14:12
☐ Saturday: Matthew 5:6
MEMORY VERSE: Now concerning spiritual gifts, brethren, I would not
have you ignorant.
—1 Corinthians 12:1
In this lesson, we will examine the gifts. In 1 Corinthians 12:1, the Apos-
tle Paul penned, "Now concerning spiritual gifts, brethren, I would not have
you ignorant." Though the congregation in Corinth came "behind in no gift"
(or as one rendering says, "There is no gift in which you are deficient"; 1 Co-
rinthians 1:7), they were lacking understanding concerning these "gifts" and
their proper operation. Certainly, if this congregation in the first century
(where all these gifts were operating) needed teaching, it is even more crucial
for the church in the twenty-first century (that is shedding the effects of the
sectarian taint of the cloudy day, Protestantism) to receive clear instruction
concerning these gifts.
What Is a Spiritual Gift?
1 Corinthians 12:1 Now concerning spiritual gifts ... I would not have
you ignorant. One rendering says, "Not right for you to be without teach-
ing." Notice the Apostle denoted these as spiritual gifts. One translation of-
fers this passage as, "I do not want you to be ignorant about manifestations
of the Spirit." The Greek word for "spiritual" in our text is pneumatikos. It
literally means "non-carnal, supernatural." This word does not appear in the
Greek Septuagint or the Gospels. It is a post-Pentecost word, indicating
those things that have their origin with God and therefore are in harmony
with His character. It describes the qualities that proceed from God's nature
and are produced in the saint's life through the Spirit of God.
Therefore, gifts that are truly spiritual gifts have a spiritual nature. The
Scripture here is not speaking of masons, carpenters, or other physical incli-
nations or talents. Certainly, children of God will sanctify these abilities to
the work of God, serving as great blessings; but these types of abilities are
not what is being dealt with in this text.
The word gifts is charisma in the original Greek. Outside of the New
Testament, this word was not in common usage. In classical Greek, it was
rarely used. In the New Testament, it is characteristically Paul's word. This
word charisma occurs seventeen times—fourteen in the Pauline letters, twice
in the Pastoral Epistles (also written by Paul), and once in 1 Peter. The
meaning of this word is that of a free and undeserved gift, something that
comes from God's nature, conveyed by God's grace, and given to God's peo-
ple. It could never have been achieved, attained, or possessed by any human
effort.
Who Has Spiritual Gifts?
Are these spiritual gifts for a spiritually elite group of people? Who is
able to have these spiritual gifts? Consider the word used by Jesus in Mat-
thew 25:15 where He declared He gave "to every man according to his sever-
al ability." Jesus indicated that "every man" receives a talent. In 1 Corinthi-
ans 7:7, the Apostle Paul substantiated this, penning, "But every man hath
his proper gift of God." In 1 Corinthians 12:11, the sacred writer revealed
the encouraging truth that "the selfsame Spirit" divides to "every man sever-
ally as he will." Not only does "every" saint receive a spiritual gift, but they
are given "according to his several ability" (the word severally means "spe-
cially assigned"; The New Analytical Greek Lexicon). What a beautiful, in-

lines.rawText: spiring truth! The Emphatic Greek Diaglott says "according to his R ESPEC -
lines.text: spiring truth! The Emphatic Greek Diaglott says "according to his RESPEC-
TIVE capacity."
Ephesians 4:7 Unto every one of us is given grace according to the
measure of the gift of Christ. As children of God, we are "all the members
of that one body" (1 Corinthians 12:12), "the church" (Colossians 1:18).
Since every member has a gift as part of the one body, "every joint supplieth"
(Ephesians 4:16); every member ministers to a need or provides a function
in the church by the operation of that particular gift. Keep in mind, although
"every one of us" has a gift, not everyone fills the offices mentioned in Ephe-
sians 4:11.
Though it requires "gifts" to be qualified to fill an office, many who have
these spiritual gifts do not fill the particular offices mentioned there. For
example, in Romans 12:8, the Apostle listed the gift of giving. Certainly, one
may have this gift and yet never receive a call to be "apostles ... prophets ...
evangelists ... pastors and teachers" (Ephesians 4:11). This reveals that all
the gifts supply a vital part to the body of Christ and that each member and
the operation of his or her gift is vital. Although he or she may not hold an
office that is particularly mentioned, the operation of his or her gift is vital
to the successful operation of the body.
The Operation of the Gifts
It should always be remembered that any gift you may have is just that—a
gift from God (James 1:17). It is nothing of which you should be proud or
boastful. The Apostle Paul declared, "But by the grace of God I am what I
am" (1 Corinthians 15:10). The gift should be operated humbly, "in honour
preferring one another" (Romans 12:10), allowing the gift to make room for
itself (Proverbs 18:16). Also, we should not allow jealousy or envy to work,

lines.rawText: as the Lord apportions "according to his R ESPECTIVE capacity" (Matthew
lines.text: as the Lord apportions "according to his RESPECTIVE capacity" (Matthew
25:15; The Emphatic Greek Diaglott). In His wisdom, the Lord knows which
gifts we are best matched to by our temperament, emotional composition, and
physical abilities.
We should not be selfish with our gifts. First Corinthians 12:7 tells us,
"But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal."
One translation says "that he may use it for the common good." Another says
"for the profit of all." The gift each saint possesses is not for his or her own
selfish benefit. Rather, as Paul told the Corinthians, "Forasmuch as ye are
zealous of spiritual gifts, seek that ye may excel to the edifying of the
church" (1 Corinthians 14:12). The Amplified Bible Classic states, "Since
you are so eager and ambitious to possess spiritual endowments and mani-
festations of the [Holy] Spirit, [concentrate on] striving to excel and to
abound [in them] in ways that will build up the church." Any time we seek
to operate our gifts, it should be divinely prompted, in divine order, and for
the benefit and edification of the body.
Dividing to Every Man
In 1 Corinthians 12:11, notice the particular wording that the Apostle em-
ployed. He declared the Spirit is "dividing [a present tense verb] to every
man." This is a continual and ongoing work of the Spirit in the church
throughout every period of time. Not only is He giving gifts and abilities to
the newly saved as they are added to the church, but in view of the Apostle's
admonition to "covet earnestly the best gifts" (1 Corinthians 12:31), if we
"hunger and thirst after righteousness" (Matthew 5:6), we "shall be filled."
If we "covet earnestly" what the Spirit is still "dividing," we can receive
additional gifts. What an encouraging thought! We can desire more spiritual
gifts. God is desirous to impart them for the betterment of His body. May we
never be satisfied but ever strive for "the best gifts."
JUST A THOUGHT
If one does not use his gift to "profit withal,"
sadly, it will not profit at all!
LESSON 3
WISDOM AND KNOWLEDGE
Scripture Text: 1 Corinthians 12:1-8
DAILY READINGS
☐ Monday: Psalm 87:1-7
☐ Tuesday: Acts 4:13-21

lines.rawText: G Wednesday: 2 Chronicles 1:10; Daniel 1:17; Proverbs 8:1; Proverbs 4:5
lines.text: ☐ Wednesday: 2 Chronicles 1:10; Daniel 1:17; Proverbs 8:1; Proverbs 4:5
☐ Thursday: Acts 6:1-10, 15
☐ Friday: Acts 18:24-28
☐ Saturday: 1 Corinthians 3:5-11
MEMORY VERSE: Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom:
and with all thy getting get understanding.
—Proverbs 4:7
Beginning with this lesson, we want to examine two particular gifts spe-
cifically mentioned in the New Testament. In our text, as well as in Romans
12:6-8, the Apostle Paul enumerated specific spiritual gifts. In these listings,
the divine penman was certainly not implying the list is exhaustive or entire.
Certainly, these gifts are central and crucial to the successful operation of the
New Testament church. However, it is also evident these passages are not
all-inclusive of all gifts. The psalmist prophesied in Psalm 87:7, "The singers
[and] ... the players on instruments shall be there." There are indeed those
who are especially gifted to be one of "the singers" or "the players."
In the Parable of the Talents, we read the gifts are distributed "according
to his several ability" (Matthew 25:15). This verse says, "And unto one he
gave five talents, to another two, and to another one." Thus, the apportion-
ment rests with the divine, and some may receive "several" gifts. These gifts
possessed by various members of the body of Christ are for a twofold pur-
pose: "mak[ing] increase of the body" and "the edifying of itself" (Ephesians
As we view the specific gifts mentioned in the Pauline epistles, we also
want to see how they were practically performed by the morning-time breth-
ren who held various offices.
The Word of Wisdom
1 Corinthians 12:8 For to one is given by the Spirit the word of wis-
dom. We must be reminded that these gifts are given. We are not talking
about natural abilities, inclinations, or propensities, but we are talking about
"gifts." In the beginning of the Gospel Day, the ministry had a number of
what was termed "unlearned and ignorant men" (Acts 4:13). The average
high school graduate today is probably much better educated than many of
the initial morning-time ministers. Yet, they "turned the world upside down"
Verse 8 speaks of the word of wisdom. The Greek word for "wisdom"
is sophia. It means "the insight into the true nature of things." The ancient
church father, Clement of Alexandria, said it is "the knowledge of things both
human and divine and of their cause." Sophia is the ultimate understanding
and insight into matters both human and divine that can only come from a di-
vine source. It enables us to understand beyond the realm of human compre-
hension and to perceive realities as they are in the spiritual and eternal
scheme. It enables the possessor of this ability or gift to act accordingly.
Solomon prayed for sophia: "Give me now wisdom [sophia]" (2 Chron-
icles 1:10). Daniel and the three Hebrew children had this wisdom as well:
"God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom" (Daniel
1:17). This particular attribute is crying for men to seek it: "Doth not wis-
dom cry? and understanding put forth her voice?" (Proverbs 8:1). The wise
man admonished us, "Get wisdom, get understanding" (Proverbs 4:5).
Let us view this gift in its New Testament setting. When the first deacons
were selected in the New Testament, the qualifications were: "men of honest
report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom" (Acts 6:3). Wisdom is a vital gift
to the successful operation of the church. When Stephen, one of the seven
deacons, disputed with the Jews, "they were not able to resist the wisdom and
the spirit by which he spake" (Acts 6:10).
The Apostle Paul said he was "a wise masterbuilder" (1 Corinthians
3:10). The wise man said, "Wisdom hath builded her house" (Proverbs 9:1).
We know this "house" is the church (Hebrews 3:6; 1 Timothy 3:15). The
Apostle Paul was successful because he had the gift of wisdom. This was ev-
ident in how he turned the Pharisees and Sadducees against each other and
diverted their attention away from him (Acts 23:6-10) and in how he admin-
istered church discipline (1 Corinthians 5:13; 2 Corinthians 2:6-8).
Paul's wisdom and patient teaching of newly established congregations is
seen in Colossians 1:3-9. Wisdom is an essential gift necessary to fill the
office of an apostle or to sow new congregations. Certainly, this gift of "the
word of wisdom" served this Apostle well as he established and nurtured
several congregations and wrote at least thirteen books of the New Testa-
ment.
The Word of Knowledge
1 Corinthians 12:8 To another the word of knowledge by the same
Spirit. Here a different gift is portrayed. The wording to another implies one
may receive the gift of "wisdom" and not receive "knowledge." Also, the con-
verse is true. One may have "all knowledge" (1 Corinthians 13:2) and not
have "the word of wisdom." However, if the Spirit sees fit, one may have
both. The Greek word for "knowledge" is gnosis. This word means "knowl-
edge of an especial kind" (The New Analytical Greek Lexicon). Jesus refer-
red to it as "the key of knowledge" (Luke 11:52). It is the ability to open
something to another, to give them entry or access into that which had pre-
viously been closed to them. In Romans 2:20, the Apostle Paul equated
"knowledge" with "the truth in the law."
Look at the words of the brethren with whom Jesus communed on the
Emmaus road: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by
the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?" (Luke 24:32). The "word
of knowledge" provides the person who possesses this gift with "the key of
knowledge," the ability to open the Scriptures to others so that truths which
were previously closed and not visible are opened and clearly seen. The
Apostle Paul, as is evident through his great host of writings, had this gift as
well (2 Corinthians 1:11).
Let us consider another brother who had this particular gift. Acts 18:24-
28 introduces a brother named Apollos. Luke, the beloved physician, said he
was "an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures" (Acts 18:24). Once
Aquila and Priscilla had "expounded unto him the way of God more per-
fectly" (Acts 18:26), it is apparent that he had "the word of knowledge." Acts
18:28 says, "He mightily convinced the Jews ... shewing by the scriptures
that Jesus was Christ." From the Apostle Paul's words, it is evident Apollos
had a little different gift than Paul. Paul said, "I have planted [that is the
work of an apostle], Apollos watered" (1 Corinthians 3:6]. Apollos was the
one who cultivated and nurtured the seed.
What office does this "word of knowledge" correlate with? Teaching.
Ephesians 4:11 says, "He gave some ... teachers." Also, "God hath set some
in the church ... thirdly teachers" (1 Corinthians 12:28). Romans 12:7 speaks
of "he that teacheth." Apollos, being "mighty in the scriptures," had this gift
of knowledge. The Holy Spirit matches the gift with the ministry and the mis-
sion that is given to its possessor. In the New Testament, Apollos was such
a renowned teacher that he was spoken of and associated with the Apostles
Paul and Peter (1 Corinthians 1:12; 3:5-6; 4:6). One noted scholar said this
about the importance of teaching: "The message of Christ needs not only
proclaimed; it needs to be explained. Exhortation and invitation without a
background of teaching are empty things."
Martin Luther and a number of scholars have attributed the writing of the
Book of Hebrews to Apollos. Whether or not this be true, he apparently had
this gift, and it served as a special benefit to the New Testament church. In
this time of evening light with the "little book open" (Revelation 10:2), the
Lord desires to impart much more knowledge. Daniel prophesied of our day
and said "knowledge shall be increased" (Daniel 12:4). This gift is very vital
to the successful operation of the church today.
JUST A THOUGHT
One must KNOW
before they are able to SHOW.
LESSON 4
FAITH, HEALING, AND MIRACLES
Scripture Text: 1 Corinthians 12:1-10
DAILY READINGS
☐ Monday: Mark 16:15-20
☐ Tuesday: Matthew 10:1, 8; 1 Corinthians 12:9-10
☐ Wednesday: Acts 3:1-11
☐ Thursday: Acts 19:10-12; Acts 20:7-12
☐ Friday: Acts 9:36-43
☐ Saturday: Acts 8:4-7; Acts 21:8
MEMORY VERSE: And they went forth, and preached every where, the
Lord working with them, and confirming the word with signs following.
—Mark 16:20
In this lesson, we will deviate from studying two gifts and mainly examine
the three gifts listed in 1 Corinthians 12:9-10. These gifts are interrelated
and are to be functional in the New Testament church for a specific purpose.
In Mark 16:17, Jesus said, "These signs shall follow them that believe." One
sign was, "They shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover" (Mark
16:18). Then, verse 20 says, "They went forth, and preached every where,
the Lord working with them, and confirming the word with signs following."

lines.rawText: The Emphatic Greek Diaglott renders it as "ratifying the W ORD through the
lines.text: The Emphatic Greek Diaglott renders it as "ratifying the WORD through the
ACCOMPANYING Signs."
These particular gifts—faith, healing, and miracles—are specifically in-
corporated into the plan of God to serve as confirmation, or ratification, of
both the truth that is being heralded and the validity of those who are herald-
ing it. This is one reason the enemy, through false religion, has seized upon
these particular gifts to make a demonstration to the public; it is their at-
tempt to claim legitimacy. In this lesson, we will examine these gifts and the
place they are ordained to fill in the furtherance of the Gospel.
1 Corinthians 12:9 To another (is given) faith by the same Spirit. In
the apportioning of the spiritual gifts, this particular faith spoken of in this
text is a gift. This is not something every child of God is given. Yes, every
child of God is "saved through faith" (Ephesians 2:8). We know when the
Holy Spirit makes His advent into the heart of a new convert, one attribute
He brings as part of "the fruit of the Spirit" is "faith" (Galatians 5:22). Also,
we know every saint has faith because we could not endure "the trying of
your faith" (James 1:3) without possessing it. However, the language of our
text is clear—this faith is not something everyone possesses. It is speaking
of a gift of faith.
An example of this gift is found in the first Christian martyr, Stephen, "a
man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost" (Acts 6:5).From the description,
clearly Stephen's faith was especially notable; he had a special gift of faith.
The account in Acts continues, "And Stephen, full of faith and power, did
great wonders and miracles among the people" (Acts 6:8). James 2:20 says,
"Faith without works is dead." Many times, the gift of faith works in con-
junction with the gifts of healing (verse 9) and the working of miracles
(verse 10).
James 2:22 instructs, "By works was faith made perfect" (the Greek trans-
lation says "complete"). Those who have this gift have a completely oper-
ational faith that can be seen in the works of healings and miracles. These
three gifts are especially used in apostolic work, in establishing the validity
of the claims of the Gospel, and in preparing an unbelieving people to hear
the Gospel. These gifts take the Gospel from a purely spiritual realm to a
natural realm that the unregenerate may behold. It is a confirmation of the
truth of the Gospel. Men may debate doctrine, argue theology, and perhaps
even question your testimony, but Acts 4:14 tells us, "Beholding the man
which was healed standing with them, they could say nothing against it."
Healing
1 Corinthians 12:9 To another the gifts of healing by the same Spirit.
This expression is unique in the sense that gifts is spoken of in the plural
tense. Everywhere this is mentioned, it is spoken of in this manner. First Co-
rinthians 12:28 speaks of "gifts of healings," and in 1 Corinthians 12:30 the
Apostle asked, "Have all the gifts of healing?" Why is it spoken of in this
manner? The Emphatic Greek Diaglott renders this phrase as "Gifts of
Cures." In Matthew 10:1, when Jesus initially commissioned the twelve, we
read, "He gave them power against unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to
heal all manner of sickness and all manner of disease." It takes a different
cure to heal disease than to heal just sickness and a different cure, yet, to
heal those vexed by unclean spirits. Each different cure is actually a different
gracious gift.
1 Corinthians 12:10 Miracles ... discerning of spirits ... kinds of
tongues are all spoken of in the plural. Needless to say, there are different
spirits and different languages, and certainly, no two miracles are exactly the
same. So it is with healing. Each healing spoken of in our text is the
operation of a unique gift fitted for the occasion or circumstance for which
it is to be manifested.
In Acts 3:1-11 is the account of the lame man at the gate Beautiful. No-
tice specifically the Apostle Peter's words: "Silver and gold have I none; but
such as I have give I thee" (verse 6). He did not say "such as John and I
have." Why? John had a different gift. Peter had the "gifts of healing." It is
worthy of mention that Peter did not pray over the lame man nor anoint him
with oil. Those are Biblical practices the elders as a whole are instructed to
engage in for healing (James 5:14), but Peter was operating a special gift or
ability.
Another "manifestation of the Spirit" is recorded in Acts 5:15. It says,
"Insomuch that they brought forth the sick into the streets, and laid them on
beds and couches, that at the least the shadow of Peter passing by might
overshadow some of them." Verse 16 says, "There came also a multitude out
of the cities round about ... bringing sick folks ... and they were healed every
one." This was another gracious gift; this was not the normal course of heal-
ing. It was a special gift. One scholar renders the phrase in 1 Corinthians
12:9 as "the special gifts of healing."
Miracles
1 Corinthians 12:10 To another the working of miracles. The Greek
word in this text is dunamis and means "power, a supernatural power." The
Apostle Paul had this gift, as evidenced in Acts 19:11-12: "And God wrought
special miracles by the hands of Paul: So that from his body were brought
unto the sick handkerchiefs or aprons, and the diseases departed from them."
We also see this in Acts 20:9-12, where a young man "fell down from the
third loft, and was taken up dead. And Paul went down, and fell on him, and
embracing him said, ... his life is in him."
The Apostle Peter had this gift as well, as we see in the raising of Tabi-
tha, or Dorcas, from the dead (Acts 9:36-42). These gifts were especially
beneficial to those with the calling to the office of an apostle. An apostle is
going into virgin areas and sowing the seed of the Gospel and attempting to
raise up new works. The manifestation of these gifts—faith, healing, and
miracles—serves as a confirmation of the Word they preach. Consider the
raising of Dorcas. Acts 9:42 tells us, "And it was known throughout all Jop-
pa; and many believed in the Lord."
It is also beneficial to an evangelist. Acts 8:6 tells us, "And the people
with one accord gave heed unto those things which Philip spake, hearing and
seeing the miracles which he did." Acts 21:8 speaks of "Philip the evange-
list." The operation of these gifts as a "manifestation of the Spirit" enables
the unregenerate, unsaved, and even sectarians (who rest on human senses
rather than the divine) to see the truth on a visible level and be convinced of
its veracity.
With a religious society about us steeped in humanism and unbelief, may
God help us to "covet earnestly the best gifts" (1 Corinthians 12:31), gifts
that can be used in the face of an unbelieving world to help sow the truth in
new localities and enable honest hearts to see where the truth is and where
they may assemble.
JUST A THOUGHT
Men can perform treatments,
but Christ performs cures.

PROPHECY AND PROPHETS
Scripture Texts: 1 Corinthians 12:10

MEMORY VERSE: Now there were in the church that was at Antioch
certain prophets and teachers.
—Acts 13:1
In this lesson, we will consider the gift of prophecy and the correspond-
ing office of the New Testament prophet. In addition to our text, we find this
gift spoken of in Romans 12:6, which states, "Having then gifts differing ac-
cording to the grace that is given to us, whether prophecy, let us prophesy."
Then, we see the corresponding office of one who has this gift (1 Corinthians
12:28-29). Ephesians 4:11 relates it as, "He gave some ... prophets."
The realms of modern religion are quick to say prophecy is an Old Testa-
ment office, now obsolete or antiquated, but in Ephesians 4:11, it is em-
ployed in the same verse as "evangelists," "pastors," and "teachers." If the
office of prophet is obsolete or relegated merely to the first century, to be
consistent, should not the other offices be obsolete as well? In truth, "the
gifts and calling of God are without repentance" (Romans 11:29). Each of
the offices (and the gifts necessary to fill them) are New Testament offices,
which are to be filled by Him that "might fill all things" (Ephesians 4:10).
Conversely, there is a rise in false religion of some declaring themselves
to be "prophets," but Deuteronomy 18:22 tells us, "If the thing follow not,

lines.rawText: nor come to pass," we will know "the L ORD hath not spoken." Also, 2 John
lines.text: nor come to pass," we will know "the LORD hath not spoken." Also, 2 John
10 admonishes, "If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, re-
ceive him not." So, we must be discerning.
1 Corinthians 12:10 To another prophecy. What is prophecy? This
term is broader than commonly realized. Prophecy involves two aspects: (1)
a foretelling of things to occur, and (2) a forth-telling (defined by The New
Analytical Greek Lexicon as "a gifted faculty of setting forth and enforcing
revealed truth ... matter of divine teaching set forth by special gift").
The First Aspect of Prophecy—Foretelling
Acts 21:10 mentions "a certain prophet, named Agabus." He was a New
Testament prophet. Was this a gift or a "manifestation of the Spirit" (1 Co-
rinthians 12:7)? Agabus prophesied to Paul, "Thus saith the Holy Ghost, So
shall the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man that owneth this girdle" (Acts
21:11). This was a foretelling. Agabus was the same prophet who "signified
by the spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world" (Acts
11:28). Verse 27 uses the term prophets in the plural: "And in these days
came prophets from Jerusalem unto Antioch." It is evident that this office is
a New Testament office, one utilized by the Spirit and filled by several in-
dividuals.
Philip the evangelist had four daughters who prophesied (Acts 21:8-9).
Clearly, this was a frequent and functional gift in the New Testament church.
The Apostle Paul had this ability as well. In 2 Thessalonians 2:3, he proph-
esied, "Let no man deceive you by any means: for that day shall not come,
except there come a falling away first." In 1 Timothy 4:1, he proclaimed,
"Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart
from the faith." In 2 Timothy 3:1, he said, "This know also, that in the last
days perilous times shall come." Here the Apostle Paul was foretelling.
The Second Aspect of Prophecy—Forth-telling
There are those who receive prophecy, and there are those who understand
prophecy and expound it. Many times, the gift incorporates both, as in the
case of John. John received "the words of the prophecy of this book" (Revela-
tion 22:18), but he also had an ability to expound on other prophecies. Con-
sider his words in 1 John 2:18, which says, "As ye have heard that antichrist
shall come [that term is not employed in the Revelation; he was expounding
on other prophecy], even now are there many antichrists; whereby we know
that it is the last time." The word prophecy in our text is the Greek word
propheteia. It comes from pro (which means "forth") and phemi (which
means "to speak"). Vine's Expository Dictionary of New Testament Words
says it means: "Speaking forth of the mind and counsel of God. It is the
declaration of that which cannot be known by natural means."
In Revelation 10:11, John was told he would eventually leave the confine-
ment on Patmos and "prophesy again before many peoples, and nations, and
tongues, and kings." It is evident John had the gift of prophecy and filled the
office of a prophet. In Revelation 22:9, John was told by the messenger of
the Revelation, "I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren the prophets."
John was numbered among the brethren who were prophets.
In today's religious confusion concerning prophecy and Revelation, proph-
ecy is a vital gift, not only to foretell what lies ahead, but to forth-tell the
previous prophecies and revelation truths that have brought the people of
God to the present-day position. The Lord desires His people to understand
prophetic truths. Prophecy is to edify and instruct the church, not "them that
believe not" (1 Corinthians 14:22; 14:4).
The Lord desires prophetic truths be forth-told to give a historical bearing
of what has occurred through the Gospel Day, of where we are, and of how
we arrived where we are today. God also desires the New Testament church
to have prophets who can tell where we are going and what yet lies ahead in
the prophetic spectrum.
Prophets—Also New Testament Office
The office of prophets was no small, unimportant office in the New Testa-
ment church. It is mentioned frequently (and in the plural) in the Book of
Acts. Acts 11:27 says, "And in these days came prophets [plural] from Jeru-
salem unto Antioch." Acts 13:1 tells us, "Now there were in the church that
was at Antioch certain prophets [plural] and teachers; as Barnabas, and
Simeon that was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen ... and
Saul." These offices of "prophets and teachers" were fully functional in the
early morning-time New Testament church.
Acts 15:32 reads, "And Judas and Silas, being prophets also themselves,
exhorted the brethren with many words, and confirmed them." In 1 Corin-
thians 14:37, the Apostle Paul said, "If any man think himself to be a prophet
...." This was clearly an accepted and functional gift and office in the first
century. It is just as vitally needed in this twenty-first century. Let us not
embrace the false thinking of sectarianism that this gift is obsolete.
All the gifts are "to profit withal" (1 Corinthians 12:7). Without the oper-
ation of each Biblical gift, the body will experience a deficiency. All "are
necessary" (1 Corinthians 12:22). If ever the saints who are scattered abroad
needed the prophetic truths heralded to expose the falsities of sectarianism
so that they can come leaping and shouting home to Zion, it is today. If ever
the church needed enlightenment on what lies before her and how to achieve
her task, it is today. The Apostle placed great importance on this gift when
he said, "Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts, but rather that ye
may prophesy" (1 Corinthians 14:1). God help us to "covet earnestly" (1 Co-
rinthians 12:31) these gifts so that the church may benefit.
JUST A THOUGHT
The gifts are "to profit withal,"
but to gain the "profit," we must be with all!
LESSON 6
DISCERNMENT AND MERCY
Scripture Texts: Romans 12:8; 1 Corinthians 12:10

MEMORY VERSE: Then shall ye return, and discern between the righteous
and the wicked, between him that serveth God and him that serveth him not.
—Malachi 3:18
In this lesson, we will consider two gifts that complement each other.
These gifts operate closely together, for it is necessary to have the one in or-
der to properly know when to dispense the other. Our text in the Corinthian
letter speaks of discerning of spirits, and in the Roman Epistle, a gift of
mercy is mentioned. It is rather astounding that mercy would be listed as a
specific gift.
Romans 12:8 He that showeth mercy [let him do it], with cheerfulness.
Rarely do we think of showing mercy as a gift, but from its inclusion in this
listing, it evidently is so. These two gifts have a correlation. Without discern-
ment, how can it be known whether a situation warrants judgment or mercy?
In a day of a specious apostasy, these two Biblical gifts are as needful to the
successful operation of the church today as they were in the first century.
A Common Salvation
Jude 3 speaks of our "common salvation," and there are several attributes
"common," or universal, to all who possess this experience of salvation. The
most familiar is that we all share "temptation ... such as is common to man"
(1 Corinthians 10:13). There are other aspects of commonality as well. The
Prophet Malachi spoke of this New Testament dispensation, declaring: "In
that day [a prophetic expression of this Gospel Day] when I make up my
jewels .... Then shall ye return, and discern between the righteous and the
wicked, between him that serveth God and him that serveth him not" (Mala-
chi 3:17-18). This prophetic passage reveals each of the "jewels," or saints,
have a certain amount of discernment; it is common to all.
In 1 Corinthians 2:15, we are told, "But he that is spiritual judgeth ['dis-
cerneth'] all things." Every spiritual person has a certain amount of discern-
ment. We are each enjoined, "Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also
is merciful" (Luke 6:36). But in this lesson's text, we see more depicted than
just the common dispensation of these abilities; we see specific gifts.
What Is Discernment?
1 Corinthians 12:10 To another discerning of spirits. Incorporating the
words "to another" indicates not everyone receives this specific gift of discer-
nment. What is this gift of discernment? First Corinthians 2:15 gives insight,
saying, "He that is spiritual judgeth all things." The Greek word for "judg-
eth" is anakrino and means "the exercise of a discerning judgment of all
things as to their true value" (Vine's Expository Dictionary of New Testa-
ment Words). It is the same word used in reference to trying one judicially
("examined," Acts 28:18; "examine," 1 Corinthians 9:3). It is the ability,
through "the manifestation of the Spirit" (1 Corinthians 12:7), of judging be-
tween that which is of the Holy Spirit and that which is prompted or promo-
ted by another spirit. It is judging between that which is divine and that
which is diabolical. One rendering of 1 Corinthians 12:10 describes it as
"the ability to distinguish between different kinds of spirits."
Examples of the Gift of Discernment
Let us consider Biblical accounts where this gift was in operation. In Acts
5:1-10, the account of Ananias and Sapphira is recorded. When they "kept
back part of the price," the only ones "privy to it" (verse 2) were Ananias and
his wife, Sapphira. Yet, when Ananias came before Peter, Peter said, "Anan-
ias, why hath Satan filled thine heart to lie to the Holy Ghost, and to keep
back part of the price of the land?" (verse 3). How did Peter know that? Ec-
clesiastes 10:20 says, "A bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which
hath wings shall tell the matter." That "bird" is symbolic of the Holy Spirit
(Matthew 3:16); the gift of discernment, given by the Holy Spirit, revealed
the matter to Peter.
Look at when the Gospel was introduced to Samaria. Acts 8:13-14 says:
"Then Simon himself believed also: and when he was baptized, he continued
with Philip [notice Philip's call was as an 'evangelist'; Acts 21:8].... Now
when the apostles [those responsible and gifted to start new works] which
were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they
sent unto them Peter and John." To understand why Peter was selected, look
at what occurred in verses 21-23. Peter discerned Simon's spirit, saying in
verse 23, "I perceive that thou art in the gall of bitterness, and in the bond of
iniquity."
Peter was sent because he had the gift of discernment. Certainly the Lord
used Philip the evangelist greatly in Samaria, but there were limitations to
his abilities, and there was a place where other members of the body needed
to operate their gifts and fill their offices. Another manifestation of discern-
ment is seen in Paul's rebuke of the "damsel possessed with a spirit of divina-
tion" (Acts 16:16). In this passage (Acts 16:16-18), the damsel spoke the
truth, but the spirit she possessed was discerned by Paul to be devilish. This
is a very necessary and important gift in the field of apostolic work. When
he goes into a new area, he does not have the time to learn or to get to know
the people as well perhaps as a pastor would. He needs to be able to discern
what he is dealing with so that he can operate appropriately.
Discernment With Mercy
Thus far, we have seen discernment operate in a manner that required re-
buke and judgment to be meted out, but there is another aspect to discern-
ment. In Acts 11:19-26, the Gospel was first purposely introduced to the
Gentiles in Antioch. When "tidings of these things came unto the ears of the
church which was in Jerusalem: ... they sent forth Barnabas" (verse 22). But
when Barnabas "came, and had seen the grace of God" (verse 23), look at
what he did. "Then departed Barnabas to Tarsus, for to seek Saul" (verse
25). Why? In Romans 11:13, Paul called himself "the apostle of the Gen-
tiles." In Antioch, the first Gentile congregation was established, and Barna-
bas discerned Paul's call to the Gentiles.
Consider the young man "John, whose surname was Mark" (Acts 15:37),
who traveled along on the first missionary trip taken by Barnabas and Saul
(Acts 13:2). "John departing from them returned to Jerusalem" (Acts 13:13).
Thus, when they were ready to take their second journey: "Barnabas deter-
mined to take with them John, whose surname was Mark. But Paul thought
not good to take him with them, who departed from them from Pamphylia,
and went not with them to the work" (Acts 15:37-38). Here we see discern-
ment working in conjunction with "he that sheweth mercy" (Romans 12:8).
John Mark, who later wrote the Gospel of Mark, was Barnabas' nephew
(Colossians 4:10). No doubt, he may have known him better than Paul, but
Barnabas also discerned something in John Mark that others did not see at
that juncture (just as he earlier discerned a special ability in Paul). Barnabas
felt it warranted mercy rather than judgment. The brethren recognized he had
this gift, for in Acts 4:36, he was "surnamed Barnabas, (which is, being in-
terpreted, The son of consolation)." Later, the Apostle Paul saw merit in
John Mark as well. Speaking of Mark in 2 Timothy 4:11, Paul said, "He is
profitable to me for the ministry," and he instructed the Colossians, "If he
come unto you, receive him" (Colossians 4:10).
If not for Barnabas' discernment and gift of showing "mercy, with cheer-
fulness" (Romans 12:8), this tender plant would have been crushed in its
growth and could never have developed into the stalwart leader that John
Mark became. There is a time for judgment and a time for mercy; discern-
ment distinguishes between these seasons. In 1 Corinthians 5:1-5, Paul ad-
monished that severe judgment be put on one who had his father's wife, but
in 2 Corinthians 2:6, he discerned, "Sufficient to such a man is this punish-
ment." He added, "Confirm your love toward him" (verse 8).
This vital gift can help a pastor know how to administer discipline. It can
aid pastors or teachers in recognizing those coming up under them whom the
Lord has His hand on. Properly exercised, this gift can reveal the devious
"Simon the Sorcerers" trying to work among us and put the proper judgment
on them. Additionally, if it is working as it ought, it can also recognize the
Apostle Pauls and John Marks whom the Lord would like to raise from ob-
scurity to the leadership of the church.
JUST A THOUGHT
Discernment can see a diamond in the rough.
Mercy works with the rough to secure the diamond.

TONGUES AND INTERPRETATION OF TONGUES

MEMORY VERSE: And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein
we were born?
—Acts 2:8
In this lesson, we will consider the last two gifts mentioned in our text: di-
vers kinds of tongues and the interpretation of tongues. These two gifts
have been greatly misrepresented and misused in the realms of religion.
Modern Pentecostal movements advocate that speaking in tongues is the
initial evidence of the Holy Ghost baptism and that this is an evidence that
all should receive. However, the writer clearly stated, "All these worketh that
one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will"
(1 Corinthians 12:11).
The questions posed in 1 Corinthians 12:30, "Do all speak with tongues?
do all interpret?" beg the obvious answer of no. No more than all are apostles
or all are prophets, as the question is posed in the preceding verse (verse 29).
It was never ordained that all would be recipients of these gifts. This explic-
itly teaches that we do not all receive the same gifts. The word "initial" does
not appear in the Scriptures, and the only place "evidence" appears in the
New Testament is in Hebrews 11:1, which declares, "Faith is ... the evidence
of things not seen." Faith is the evidence, not a manifestation of "tongues."
What Are "Divers Kinds of Tongues"?
1 Corinthians 12:10 To another divers kinds of tongues. The sacred
writer informed us in his elaboration on "diversities of gifts" (1 Corinthians
12:4) that there is one gift known as divers kinds of tongues. One rendering
expresses it: "Still another person is able to speak in languages he never
learned." The word divers in The Expanded Greek Translation of the New
Testament is "various." The phrase is offered as "various kinds of lan-
guages." The Emphatic Greek Diaglott says "different languages." This gift
is not speaking in some unintelligible manner but rather in a language under-
stood by the hearer.
Biblical Examples
Scriptures list three explicit occasions where this gift was in operation.
The most famous account is the Day of Pentecost, so called because it was
a Jewish feast (Feast of Pentecost). The word Pentecost comes from the
Greek word pentekoste and literally means "fiftieth." The Feast of Pentecost
derived its name because it was fifty days after the Jewish Feast of Passover.
Several truths are notable in this account (Acts 2:1-38). Verse 4 says they
"began to speak with other tongues" (the Greek word is glossa, which means
"languages"), and verse 6 says that "every man heard them speak in his own
language." Several truths are here revealed about this gift.
First, the languages they heard were understandable. Verse 11 says, "We
do hear them speak in our tongues [or languages] the wonderful works of
God." Second, the purpose for the gift is revealed, which was to communi-
cate the Gospel. Third, when the spiritual gift of languages is operating,
there is no need of interpretation. In each of the three instances where we see
this gift operating, these three truths are substantiated (Acts 2:1-38; 10:44-
In Acts 2:9-11, sixteen distinct localities or ethnic groups are enumerated.
In verse 14, we read, "But Peter, standing up with the eleven, lifted up his
voice, and said unto them, ... hearken to my words." Then, in verses 15-36,
he preached the Gospel. Verse 37 tells us, "Now when they heard this, they
were pricked in their heart." His message was understandable to all sixteen
dialects. Yet, Acts 4:13 informs us Peter was "unlearned and ignorant," as
far as formal education was concerned. This was the operation of a gift; Pe-
ter spoke, and they each heard him "speak in our tongues" (Acts 2:11).
It is important to note that while Paul wrote in 1 Corinthians 14:18, "I
speak with tongues more than ye all," there is no scriptural evidence he had
the gift of languages. Although one may have gained the ability through edu-
cation to speak in different languages, that is not the gift mentioned in our
lesson text. It is obvious in the three accounts in Acts that it was the oper-
ation of this gift. It is beyond the scope of this study, but it should be men-
tioned that the "unknown tongue" spoken of in 1 Corinthians, Chapter 14,
has nothing to do with this gift. It refers to the practice that was taking place
in Corinth—ones speaking in a language they knew but was unknown to the
hearers.
Why Were Tongues Used?
The three instances where the employment of this gift are listed were
historic occasions. Acts, Chapter 2, explains that the truth was introduced
to "Jews, devout men" (verse 5); it was introduced to the Jewish nation. In
the case at Cornelius' house, it was a confirmation that the new covenant in-
corporated "the Gentiles" (Acts 10:45; 11:17-18). The Gospel reached the
full spectrum of men when the twelve Samaritan disciples at Ephesus em-
braced the message "and prophesied" (Acts 19:1-7), or the Twentieth Cen-
tury New Testament says "to preach" (Acts 19:6). (Dr. Lawrence J. Chest-
nut, in his book True Bible Tongues, devotes the entirety of Chapter 10 to
what he denotes as "the twelve Samaritans at Ephesus.") This gift is to be
used to communicate by declaration or acceptance of the Gospel.
In Genesis 11:1-9, when men aspired to build their own way to "reach
unto heaven" (verse 4), God said, "Let us go down, and there confound their
language, that they may not understand one another's speech" (verse 7). A

lines.rawText: condition was created where "the L ORD scattered them" (verse 8), and "the
lines.text: condition was created where "the LORD scattered them" (verse 8), and "the
name of it [was] called Babel ["Confusion"; the Septuagint]" (verse 9). In the
three instances we are studying of first century civilization embracing the
truth, we see a return to "that which was from the beginning" (1 John 1:1).
Through the Gospel and its acceptance, men from "every nation under
heaven" (Acts 2:5) were brought back into unity and able to understand one
another by the operation of this spiritual gift. This is why it occurred on
three occasions and to three distinct groups: the Jews, the Gentiles, and the
Samaritans (a mixed race of Jew and Gentile). These three accounts substan-
tiate the truth of Acts 10:35, which reads, "But in every nation he that fear-
eth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him."
Yet today, if a language barrier exists and impairs the ability to communi-
cate the Gospel, this gift can be a "manifestation of the Spirit" (1 Corinthians
12:7) to enable the speaker to preach in a language previously unknown to
him and to communicate the Gospel. It still acts as a confirmation of the
Word (Mark 16:17-20).
The Gift of Interpretation
1 Corinthians 12:10 To another the interpretation of tongues. This is
another of the spiritual gifts spoken of in this chapter. While 1 Corinthians,
Chapter 14, speaks of an "interpreter" (verse 28) and of "let[ting] one inter-
pret" (verse 27), that does not necessarily indicate a spiritual gift. One may
be able to interpret a language because of his familiarity with it or because
of educational training. The "interpretation" mentioned in our text is a gift.
Interpretation in our text is hermeneia in the Greek language and means
"translation." Hermeneia comes from the Greek word Hermes, the Greek
name of the pagan god Mercury, who was regarded as the messenger of the
gods. It denotes "to explain" and is used for explaining the meaning of words
in a different language" (Vine's Expository Dictionary of New Testament
Words).
Though not a New Testament account, we see an example of interpre-
tation in Daniel, Chapter 5. Daniel 5:5 says, "Fingers of a man's hand ...
wrote over against the candlestick upon the plaister of the wall." The wise
men of Babylon "could not read the writing, nor make known to the king the
interpretation" (Daniel 5:8). The ministers in spiritual Babylon still cannot
read the Word and understand its message yet today. But Daniel had "an ex-
cellent spirit" (Daniel 5:12), and he interpreted the message of truth (Daniel
The purpose of the New Testament gift of interpretation is to make the
truth understandable to the masses when it is sent in a language they do not
understand. Today, one may travel to foreign soil to encourage missionary
work, be unable to speak their language, and not have the gift of languages.
In those cases, the Lord will use those with the gift of interpretation so that
God's Word may be understood. These gifts are needed yet today. The field
is still the world (Matthew 13:38), and the commission is still, "Go ye into
all the world" (Mark 16:15). As long as there are language barriers, there
will be a need for the operation of these gifts.
JUST A THOUGHT
The evidence of the Holy Ghost
is a holy life!

MINISTRY AND HELPS

MEMORY VERSE: And let these also first be proved; then let them use the
office of a deacon, being found blameless.
—1 Timothy 3:10
We have completed our study of the gifts enumerated in 1 Corinthians
12:8-10; however, there are additional gifts mentioned in Romans 12:6-8 and
in 1 Corinthians 12:28 that warrant our consideration.
Romans 12:7 Or ministry, let us wait on our ministering. And a small
but very important word is inserted in our companion text: helps (1 Corin-
thians 12:28). The word helps is a small word, yet it fills a large need in and
amongst the Christian community. In the original Greek, the word for "helps"
is antilepsis. It is a compound word, composed from two root words: anti
(which means "in exchange") and lambano (which means "to take, lay hold
of, so as to support"). Vine's Expository Dictionary of New Testament
Words tells us it is "one of the ministrations of the local church, by way of
rendering assistance, perhaps especially of help ministered to the weak and
needy." According to the semantics of the word, it is one who takes or lays
hold of a burden to exchange his time and efforts to help and support others.
The New Analytical Greek Lexicon defines antilepsis as "one who aids
and assists." This is an important gift in any locality. Those who are called
"continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word" (Acts 6:4) cannot
give the due devotion and attention to those spiritual functions if they are dis-
tracted by "the daily ministration" (Acts 6:1) or "the daily service" (The Em-
phatic Greek Diaglott).
Every pastor in every locality needs those who, though not perhaps called
to preach per se or maybe even to teach a class on a regular basis, feel the
burden for and receive the gift of helps. These may work with the outcasts
in a community, prepare meals at the time of a funeral, or minister to sick or
needy saints. The corresponding verb to the word antilepsis is in the follow-
ing passages: "support the weak" (Acts 20:35); "do them service" (1 Timothy
6:2); and "holpen [helped] his servant" (Luke 1:54). For the successful oper-
ation of the church in any community, it is necessary for this gift to be oper-
ating. Without this gift, it appears to those observing that, although an ex-
cellent Biblical message is preached, it is poorly translated into practical
service to reach the level where many human needs reside.
Examples of Helpers
We marvel at the great Gospel work wrought by the Apostle Paul. We
read of his accomplishments and stand in awe at the depth and divinity of his
writings. Yet, we must not lose sight of the fact that for him to be able to do
those many things, he had to have a great host of helpers. Acts 21:8 speaks
of "we that were of Paul's company." For a pastor to devote his attention to
"prayer, and to the ministry of the word" (Acts 6:4), or for an evangelist to
travel to a locality and spend time in the prayer closet and study, there needs
to be a "company" who feels a burden and has a gift to step up and perform
other functions and fill other needs. Paul was blessed with such helpers.
In Romans 16:3, Paul penned, "Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in
Christ Jesus." In Romans 16:9, Paul said, "Salute Urbane, our helper in
Christ." In 1 Corinthians 16:15, he spoke of "the house of Stephanas ... that
they have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints." The Amplified
Bible Classic renders it, "How they have consecrated and devoted themselves
to the service of the saints (God's people)." Another rendering says, "They
have laid themselves out to be of help to Christ's people." Then in 1 Corin-
thians 16:16, Paul made a startling statement: "That ye submit yourselves
unto such, and to every one that helpeth with us, and laboureth."
The Amplified Bible Classic makes this pronouncement in verse 16 more
clear, saying, "I urge you to pay all deference to such leaders and to enlist
under them and be subject to them." Certainly, a local work deficient in those
who are helpers is limited in the scope of outreach and service, not only to
their own but to the community they are attempting to reach. This gift of
helps has two facets: its physical aspect in supporting temporal matters and
its spiritual aspect in supporting the saints and the ministry.
It is obvious, many times these "helpers" also help in the spiritual aspect
when the need arises. Stephen labored in that aspect when he presented the
truth to the Sanhedrin (Acts 7:1-53). Priscilla and Aquila engaged in more
than the physical aspect as they took Apollos aside "and expounded unto him
the way of God more perfectly" (Acts 18:26). So one who has this gift of
helps may fill a pulpit for an absent pastor, teach a class in the absence of
a teacher, or help in other spiritual capacities that may need to be filled for
a space of time.
The successful operation of this gift is recorded in Acts 6:1-7. We read,
"The twelve ... said, It is not reason that we should leave the word of God,
and serve tables" (verse 2). So the brethren appointed "seven men of honest
report, full of the Holy Ghost ... over this business" (verse 3).
What Is Ministry?
Romans 12:7 Or ministry, let us wait on our ministering. This portrays
the office filled by the one with the gift of "helps." The Greek word for mini-
stry is diakonia. It is the same word used in Acts 6:1, "ministration." It is al-
so found in Romans 15:31 as "service," in 2 Corinthians 9:1 as "ministering
to the saints," and in 2 Corinthians 9:12 as "administration of ... service."
Perhaps what gives the greatest insight is that it is a form of the word from
which the English word deacon comes. When Paul set forth the requirements
for the office of a deacon in 1 Timothy 3:8-13, the word used for "deacon"
is diakonos. So in our text, this ministry is actually the office of a deacon.
Those selected in Acts 6:3 are commonly referred to as the Seven Deacons.
Some have mistakenly used this text from the Roman Epistle to say ones
should just sit and wait for some event to occur that would propel them into
a position. One scholar made this passage less vague when he renders it as,
"If we have received the gift of practical service, let us use it in service." The
word wait in our text is not a passive word but means "to look for." We are
to look for opportunities to be of service. In the morning-time church, this
office was an accepted and functional office. In Philippians 1:1, the Apostle
wrote, "To all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi, with the bish-
ops and deacons." For the Word of God to prosper in any locality, it is vital
this office be filled. We may call them by other titles; regardless, we must
have those who fill this role. Unless there are those who tend to this aspect
of the work of God, the pastor will become overburdened, distracted, and too
pressed for time to "feed the church of God" (Acts 20:28).
Qualifications
Though it is vital to covet the gift of helps and fill the office of a deacon,
it is also necessary to be aware of Biblical requirements and the reasons for
them. These people may be the most visible examples in the community they
are attempting to win. Hence, they should be examples of the message and
truth that is preached. Second Timothy 2:6 says, "The husbandman that
laboureth must be first partaker of the fruits." If those who have this gift and
fill this office indeed meet the Biblical qualifications, they can have "great
boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus" (1 Timothy 3:13).
As Stephen the deacon, they can be effective in such a manner that people
are unable "to resist the wisdom and the spirit" by which they speak (Acts
6:10). There is a great need in every locality for people to desire the gift of
helps, serve in practical service, and be willing to engage in spiritual services
whenever it is needed.
JUST A THOUGHT
The greatest ability the Lord needs
is AVAILABILITY!
LESSON 9
EXHORTETH AND GIVETH
Scripture Text: Romans 12:8

☐ Tuesday: 2 Timothy 4:13; 1 Timothy 6:12

MEMORY VERSE: But exhort one another daily, while it is called To day;
lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.
—Hebrews 3:13
This lesson focuses on two gifts specifically spoken of in our Scripture
text: he that exhorteth and he that giveth. We do not commonly think of
these as gifts, but Romans 12:6 says, "Having then gifts differing according
to the grace that is given to us." Notice, this verse begins the particular topic
of gifts, and verses 6-8 are all one sentence. This teaches that the compon-
ents of these verses are all parts of a whole. They are all dealing with the
same tenor of thought—the gifts.
Exhortation
As a gift, this particular ability transcends a specific office. In 2 Timothy
4:2, Timothy was admonished to "exhort with all long suffering and doc-
trine," and in verse 5, he was instructed to "do the work of an evangelist."
Part of "the work of an evangelist" is to "exhort." Acts 11:22-23 says,
"Barnabas ... exhorted them all," and Acts 13:1 mentions "teachers; as
Barnabas." We know he was not one of the "prophets" (Acts 13:1) because
Acts 11:27 says, "In these days came prophets from Jerusalem unto
Antioch." Barnabas was already at Antioch, and his role was that he "taught
much people" (Acts 11:26). So we see evangelists exhort and teachers exhort.
In 1 Peter 5:1, Peter said, "The elders which are among you I exhort," and
1 Peter 1:1 styles him as "Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ." The ability to
exhort works through many offices. It is obviously an important gift for the
Apostle Paul admonished the young minister, Timothy, to "give attendance
... to exhortation" (1 Timothy 4:13).
What Is Exhortation?
Romans 12:8 Or he that exhorteth, on exhortation. The Greek word
"exhorteth" (verb) is parakaleo, which means "to encourage, comfort, con-
sole" (The New Analytical Greek Lexicon). Thayer's Greek-English Lexicon
of the New Testament says "to console, to encourage and strengthen by con-
solation, to comfort." This was obviously one gift Barnabas possessed. Acts
4:36 refers to him as "The son of consolation" (or "the son of encourage-
ment"; The Expanded Greek Translation of the New Testament).
The words parakaleo (exhorteth) and paraklesis (exhortation) are akin to
the word parakletos, which is used for the Holy Spirit, who is called "the
Comforter" (John 14:26). The word rendered in our text as "exhorteth" is
translated "comforted" (Matthew 2:18; 5:4; 2 Corinthians 1:4) and as "com-
forteth" (2 Corinthians 1:4). This portrays at least a couple of vital truths.
One, although one may be an apostle, an evangelist, or a teacher, and be en-
trusted with great abilities or insights, he must never lose sight of the fact
that he is dealing with human creatures with feelings and emotions, who are
often irrational beings needing to be encouraged, consoled, and comforted
from time to time.
It also portrays a deeper truth. In the Greek language, the word "Com-
forter" is parakletos, but in Latin, it is fortis, from which our English word
fortify comes. It means "to make brave, to strengthen." Truly anointed exhor-
tation consoles and comforts by sending inspiration that strengthens ones,
making them brave, and assuring them that through the Holy Spirit, they can
continue victoriously. Each message and lesson should be delivered with
words that lift and inspire to bravery in this "good fight of faith" (1 Timothy
The Gift of Giving
Romans 12:8 He that giveth, let him do it with simplicity. What an un-
usual gift! The Greek word for "giveth" is metadidomi and means "share" or
"impart." It is the same word used in Romans 1:11, which says, "That I may
impart unto you some spiritual gift." It is also translated in this manner in
Luke 3:11 and 1 Thessalonians 2:8. This is a portrayal of a gift where ones
will impart, or share, that which they have been entrusted with for the work
of the Gospel. This goes from the most basic "distributing to the necessity of
saints" (Roman 12:13; 2 Corinthians 9:1-15) to the selling of one's excess to
provide funds to support the ministry in the propagation of the Gospel.
Acts 4:32 reads, "The multitude of them that believed were of one heart
and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things [plural]
which he possessed was his own." Verse 34 says, "For as many ['of them that
believed'; verse 32] as were possessors of lands [plural] or houses [plural]
sold them," and verse 35 says they "laid them down at the apostles' feet."
Certainly, not all who "believed" (verse 32) had the gift of giving, but this
text is a vital portrayal of the principle that lies behind Christian giving.
This passage in Acts has many times been viewed improperly. Notice,
these believers were possessors "of lands or houses" (verse 34) in the plural.
No doubt, some believers were more financially endowed than others. Ro-
mans 12:1 says the Lord only asks for "your reasonable service." These were
not being asked or compelled to sell their homes. Rather, those who had
"lands" or "houses" (plural) sold of their excess with which they had been
blessed and brought it to the Apostles for distribution. It is evident the saints
still owned homes from several Scriptures written subsequently to this (Acts
12:12; 21:8; 28:30; Romans 16:5; Colossians 4:15; Philemon 2, 22).
Many people are of the impression that the primitive church lived in a
communal setting—having sold everything they had—and were fed and kept
by the church. This is an erroneous conception of what actually occurred.
Acts 5:1 clarifies it: "But a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his
wife, sold a possession." Why did they do this? Acts 4:33 says, "And with
great power gave the apostles witness of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus:
and great grace was upon them all [the Apostles]." Verse 34 says, "Neither
was there any among them [Who has he been speaking of? The Apostles.]
that lacked [why?]; for as many as were possessors ... sold ... and brought
the prices of the things that were sold."
Verse 35 tells, "And laid them down at the apostles' feet." They were
selling of their excess to provide funds to supply the Apostles so that they
could carry the Gospel forth. In our day, ones have felt led to sell farms or
other possessions and give to support mission fields and missionaries. This
is a very needful gift in the work of God. No doubt, the work of God could
advance at a much quicker pace if those who were capable would support
apostles going forth, sowing the seed, and planting new congregations. No
doubt, evangelists could go out into the field if they were enabled financially
and did not feel compelled to hold secular jobs to support their families.
When someone is called to fill one of the offices of "apostles ... prophets
... evangelists" (Ephesians 4:11), another—who has been blessed with the
wherewithal to do so—may be given this gift of giving to provide the means
for one to financially labor in the field. Today many small congregations that
need to be evangelized and encouraged cannot afford to call an evangelist,
and the evangelist cannot afford to go due to financial constraints. There is
a great need for he that giveth to provide support to further the Gospel.
Our text says, He that giveth, let him do it with simplicity, or with hon-
esty of aim, purpose, integrity, without any mixture of a selfish purpose.
When one gives, it should be "as to the Lord" (Colossians 3:23).
JUST A THOUGHT
If you give as unto the Lord,
you will be blessed, regardless of
what is done with what is given.

RULETH AND GOVERNMENTS
Scripture Texts: Romans 12:8; 1 Corinthians 12:28

☐ Tuesday: Zechariah 2:8; 1 Corinthians 14:33; 1 Corinthians 14:40

MEMORY VERSE: Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit
yourselves: for they watch for your souls.
—Hebrews 13:17
Next, let us consider two gifts under great assault from the enemy of souls
that are absolutely essential to the divine operation of the New Testament
church. In Romans 12:8, the inspired penman admonished, he that ruleth,
with diligence. In the companion text, in 1 Corinthians 12:28 he spoke of
governments. Jesus prophesied of a time when "because iniquity [the Greek
word anomia means 'contempt and violation of the law'] shall abound, the
love of many shall wax cold" (Matthew 24:12). Many today are contemptu-
ous of people in authority, and they "despise government" (2 Peter 2:10). So
it is vitally necessary to understand the role these gifts play in the theocratic
governance of the church.
What Is Meant by "Ruleth"?
Romans 12:8 He that ruleth, with diligence. What does the term ruleth
actually mean? The Greek word is proistemi, and according to Thayer's
Greek-English Lexicon of the New Testament, it means "to set on place
before; to set over; to be over ... preside over." The New Analytical Greek
Lexicon says "to set over, appoint with authority." It is the same Greek word
used in 1 Thessalonians 5:12, which reads, "Know them which labour among
you, and are over you [proistemi] in the Lord." It is also employed in 1 Tim-
othy 5:17. "Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double hon-
our." However, another way it is used gives an insight as to one of the offices
for which this gift is very beneficial. This same Greek word is rendered
"maintain" in Titus 3:8 and 14.
God is infinitely a God of order. From the vast galaxies to the minute
atoms and molecular structures, everything of divine creation is of the most
perfect order. Should the church, the apex of His creation, "the apple of his
eye" (Zechariah 2:8), be any less so? Certainly not! God "is not the author
of confusion" (1 Corinthians 14:33). He desires that "all things be done de-
cently and in order" (1 Corinthians 14:40). For this to be so, there must be
people whom God gifts and calls to keep the order. In the face of conflicting
ideas and a real enemy who is ever trying to hinder and stymie the church,
there must be those who have authority.
First, this gift to rule or "be over" with "authority" is befitting to an apos-
tle. The Apostle Paul told the Corinthians: "For though ye have ten thousand
instructers in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers [one rendering says 'you
have only one father']: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the
gospel. Wherefore I beseech you, be ye followers of me" (1 Corinthians 4:15-
16). One who fathers, or establishes, a work in truth does the work of an
apostle and has an authority that goes with that calling.
The authority of an apostle is wider than a particular locality. In 2 Corin-
thians 11:28, Paul mentioned "that which cometh upon me daily, the care of
all the churches" (Greek, congregations). One rendering says, "I have the
daily burden of responsibility." We see this working very well in foreign
fields.
The next office for which this gift is necessary is a pastor. Notice that one
meaning of the Greek word proistemi is "maintain." Once a work is estab-
lished, there must be someone qualified and capable to oversee that work and
maintain order. Yes, growth is important, but maintenance is important as
well. A pastor is to maintain that which the apostle started and to carry the
work on. In order for divine order to function as intended, those in positions
of oversight need to be honored and obeyed. (See Hebrews 13:7, 17.) Sub-
mitting to divinely appointed authority is essential for the operation of theo-
cratic government.
Governments
1 Corinthians 12:28 And God hath set some in the church ... govern-
ments. In tandem with the gift of ruleth, or oversight, is what Paul men-
tioned as governments. The Greek word (kubernesis) does not appear any-
where else in the New Testament. This unique word literally means "to
steer," as in the pilotage of a ship. Vine's Expository Dictionary of New Tes-
tament Words defines it as "those who act as guides in a local church." A
pilot is not the captain of the ship nor is he responsible for its voyage; but
when the ship reaches a certain portion of the water, the pilot performs a
special function.
It is obvious from the wording in this verse that the mention of govern-
ments is distinct from "apostles ... prophets ... teachers." The New Analyti-
cal Greek Lexicon defines the word governments as "office of a ... director."
One translation says "administrator" and another "manager." One scholar
says, "Paul is referring to the people who carry out administration of the
church." These are those who hold special areas of authority in a local con-
gregation. They work under the auspices of the pastor. We might call these
people Sunday school superintendents, song leaders or music directors, choir
directors, and youth leaders. This could also encompass radio ministers,
nursing home visitation coordinators, or any area of the work of God that has
a particular function or ministry and requires a specific gift, burden, and
oversight.
Notice that the term governments is in the plural. Every congregation
needs several of these types of leaders. Pastors (those who have the over-
sight—"the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers"; Acts 20:28) have the re-
sponsibility and authority to determine, under divine direction, whom they
"may appoint over" (Acts 6:3) each area of governments or responsibility
in a congregation.
Submission
For the work of God to function as the Lord desires, we must submit to
those in the various positions of authority. Without authority, there would be
chaos. To have order, there must be people in authority. Any thinking person
will come to conclusions and form opinions. To do so is totally natural.
Where it becomes dangerous is when one airs opinions that are contrary to
the leaders. Then it can become sowing "discord among brethren" (Proverbs
6:19), one of the things that the Lord hates (Proverbs 6:16). A leader may
not always move as we think he or she should or make the decision we feel
should be made. This is where submission comes into focus.
As long as we agree, there is no need to practice submission; submission
comes into focus when we disagree. We must hold our peace and yield to the
will and direction of the leader to be submissive. The work of God is too vast
and has too many facets for the pastor personally to oversee every area.
Therefore, he must place leaders in positions to oversee specific areas of the
work. Today, spirits try to wreak havoc in the work of God. People may not
contest a pastor personally or directly but instead will raise up and contest
one of these other leaders. We need to be "easy to be intreated" (James 3:17).
Consider the welfare of the body as a whole and submit for the work's sake.
Conclusion
These gifts—ruleth and governments—are vital to the proper operation
of the church. He that ruleth is dealing with the wider authority exercised
in conjunction with the office of an apostle or pastor. But governments is
extremely important to the operation of a successful local work. To cooper-
ate with these is to work for the common cause, while to work against these
is to work against Christ and the ministries of His body.
JUST A THOUGHT
It is easier to obey them that have the ruler
than to be overcome by a new ruler.

APOSTLES AND EVANGELISTS

lonians 2:6
